Stressing the wrong syllable, such as dee-kun-tek-STOO-uh-lyze; the main stress is on TEKST.

senses.definition: The act of injuring another person's reputation by any slanderous communication, written or oral; the wrong of maliciously injuring the good name of another.
senses.example: She sued his ex-boyfriend for defamation and is seeking $14,000.

core.definition: The act of damaging someone's reputation by saying or writing false statements about them, which can be a legal wrong.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on MAY, the third-to-last syllable area. The second syllable 'fuh' is very reduced, so don't pronounce it as a full 'fah'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names a harmful act, often in legal or journalistic settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use defamation mostly in legal, journalistic, and formal contexts, such as lawsuits or news stories about a public figure. In casual conversation people usually say someone 'badmouthed' or 'spread lies about' another person. Spoken, the word can sound stiff, so use 'lies' or 'rumors' in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Slander refers to spoken defamation, while defamation covers both spoken and written false statements.
Libel is written or published defamation, a more specific legal term in American law.
Criticism can be harsh but is an honest opinion, while defamation involves false statements of fact.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is threatening to sue me for defamation because I told people he was dishonest.
examples.professional: Our legal team reviewed the press release to make sure it could not be read as defamation of the former contractor.
examples.analytical: Defamation law balances the protection of a person's reputation against the public interest in free speech and open debate.

nuance.analogy: Like a rumor that spreads like wildfire: once it is out, the damage to a reputation is hard to put out.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'diffamare', 'to spread ill report', from 'dis-' (apart) and 'fama' (report, reputation).
common_mistakes: Confusing 'defamation' with 'defamatory' (the noun names the act, the adjective describes the statement).
Stressing the wrong syllable as 'DEF-uh-mation' instead of 'def-uh-MAY-shun'.

senses.definition: The act of conveying something.
senses.example: The delivery was completed by four.

senses.definition: The item which has been conveyed.
senses.example: Your delivery is on the table.

senses.definition: The manner of speaking or singing.
senses.example: The actor's delivery was flawless.

senses.definition: The process of throwing a stone.
Process of introducing foreign DNA into host cells.
A cross or pass.
The act or process of a mother giving birth.
senses.example: The delivery was painful.

senses.definition: A pitching motion.
senses.example: His delivery has a catch in it.

senses.definition: A thrown pitch.
senses.example: Here is the delivery; ... strike three!

senses.definition: The administration of a drug.
senses.example: drug delivery system

senses.definition: A ball bowled.

core.definition: The act of bringing goods, mail, or food to a person or place, often to their home or business.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on LIV. The middle syllable is often dropped or very weak, so the word sounds like 'dih-LIV-ree' in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: In American life, delivery is used all the time for food from restaurants, packages from online orders, and groceries. People often say they want delivery or have something delivered. It also has a speaking sense: a speaker's delivery means the manner in which they speak.

distinctions.note: Delivery means someone brings the item to you, while pickup means you go to the store or restaurant to collect it.
Shipping refers to the process or cost of sending goods, while delivery is the actual arrival of the items.

examples.everyday: We ordered pizza for delivery tonight, so just let me know when the driver shows up.
examples.professional: Our on-time delivery rate dropped last month, so the operations team is reviewing the warehouse schedule.
examples.analytical: A sermon's delivery may matter as much as its content, since tone and pacing shape how listeners receive the argument.

nuance.analogy: Delivery is like a mail carrier at your door: the thing you wanted comes to you, no trip required.
nuance.etymology: From deliver, from Latin liberare, to set free, through Old French delivrer.
common_mistakes: Using deliver as a noun, as in I want a deliver; the noun is delivery.
Stressing the last syllable instead of LIV.

delivery.etymology: From Middle English *deliveri* et al. from Anglo-Norman, from Old French *delivrer*.

conversation.text: Does this place do delivery, or do we have to pick it up?
The delivery fee was almost as much as the food.
Our delivery is running late, so let's start with the salad.
We're waiting for a furniture delivery between noon and four.
Delivery drivers always leave stuff at the wrong door.
Let's just order delivery tonight; I'm too tired to cook.
When is the delivery scheduled for the new couch?
Delivery is free if you live within ten miles of the store.
I missed the delivery, so they left a note on my door.

senses.definition: Deserted and devoid of inhabitants.
senses.example: a desolate isle; a desolate wilderness; a desolate house

senses.definition: Barren and lifeless.
Made unfit for habitation or use because of neglect, destruction etc.
senses.example: desolate altars

senses.definition: Dismal or dreary.
Sad, forlorn and hopeless.
senses.example: He was left desolate by the early death of his wife.

senses.definition: To deprive of inhabitants.
To devastate or lay waste somewhere.
To abandon or forsake something.
To make someone sad, forlorn and hopeless.

core.definition: Empty of people and life; deserted, barren, or bleak, often because of neglect or destruction.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the middle vowel to a schwa so it sounds like 'DES-uh-lit.' The verb is pronounced 'DES-uh-layt,' so the stress and final vowel differ between the forms.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests emptiness, loneliness, or hopelessness, and it can describe places, moods, or situations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'desolate' most often to describe a remote landscape, an abandoned town, or a bleak feeling of loneliness, as in 'a desolate highway.' It is somewhat elevated, so in casual speech people often say 'empty,' 'deserted,' or 'bleak' instead. It is natural in writing, news stories about disasters, and descriptions of nature. A natural reply to a description of a desolate place is 'That sounds pretty lonely.'

distinctions.note: 'Deserted' says a place has no people; 'desolate' also suggests it is bleak, barren, or sad.
'Barren' emphasizes the lack of growth or fertility; 'desolate' emphasizes emptiness and gloom.
'Lonely' describes a person's feeling; 'desolate' can describe a place or a feeling of total emptiness.

examples.everyday: We drove through a desolate stretch of Nevada desert with no gas stations for miles.
examples.professional: The site was desolate after the plant closed, so the city plans to rebuild the district from scratch.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard's description of the modern soul as desolate exposes a despair that no social progress can cure.

nuance.analogy: A desolate place is like a house after everyone has moved out: the rooms are still there, but nothing living remains.
nuance.etymology: From Latin desolatus, past participle of desolare, 'to leave alone or abandon,' from de- 'completely' and solare 'to make alone.'
common_mistakes: Using the verb pronunciation for the adjective (DES-uh-layt instead of DES-uh-lit).
Using 'desolate' for a simply quiet place, when it implies bleakness.
Confusing 'desolate' with 'desolated' in sentences where a participle is needed.

senses.definition: Relaxing of tension, especially between countries; an instance of this.

core.definition: A easing of hostility or tension between countries, especially rival powers, usually through talks or agreements.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the last syllable, TAHNT, and say the a like the vowel in father. Do not add a final ay or pronounce the t as a strong sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It names a improvement in relations, though the agreement may be fragile.
nuance.usage_note: Detente is used mainly in politics, diplomacy, and history, such as the Cold War detente between the United States and the Soviet Union. Americans rarely use it in casual talk. In everyday speech people say relations are improving or things calmed down.

distinctions.note: A truce is a short, specific pause in fighting; detente is a broader, longer easing of hostility between nations.
Peace means the absence of war; detente describes a relaxed relationship that may still involve rivalry.

examples.everyday: My uncle says the two families have finally reached a sort of detente since the wedding.
examples.professional: The diplomatic team hopes the trade talks will lead to a lasting detente between the two countries.
examples.analytical: Detente is best understood not as peace but as a managed rivalry in which both sides limit their competition.

nuance.analogy: Detente is like two neighbors who stop yelling over the fence and agree to keep the peace, even though they still do not like each other.
nuance.etymology: From French détente, a relaxing, from détendre, to relax, from Latin distendere, to stretch apart.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a final ay sound, as day-TAHNT-ay.
Using detente for any calm; it refers specifically to easing tension between rival states.

senses.definition: A mournful poem or piece of music composed or performed as a memorial to a deceased person.
A song or piece of music that is considered too slow, bland or boring.
To sing dirges.

core.definition: A slow, sad song, poem, or piece of music written or performed to mourn someone who has died.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a stressed er vowel, like the r-colored vowel in bird. The final j sound is soft; do not add an extra vowel after the d.

nuance.connotation: negative or somber; it describes grief, death, and mourning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dirge mostly in writing, reviews, or literary talk. In a casual conversation, you might hear it about a sad song ('That album is a dirge'). Describing a sad funeral song as a dirge is natural, but using it for something merely boring is informal and somewhat figurative.

distinctions.note: An elegy is a formal poem mourning a person; a dirge can be music or a song, and it need not be a poem.
A requiem is a Mass or musical setting for the dead in the Catholic tradition; a dirge is a more general mournful piece.

examples.everyday: The band's new song sounds like a dirge, so I'd skip it if you want something upbeat.
examples.professional: The producer said the demo drags too much, and the second verse plays like a dirge instead of a ballad.
examples.analytical: The poem works as a dirge, but its refusal to name the dead turns mourning into a meditation on loss itself.

nuance.analogy: A dirge is a slow walk behind a casket: each step is heavy and every note is grief.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dirige, 'direct,' the first word of a Psalm antiphon sung at the Office of the Dead.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with an extra vowel, as DUR-jee
Using it as a word for any slow song, when it implies mourning

dirge.etymology: From Middle English *dirige*, from Latin *dirige* (“steer, direct”), from the beginning of the first antiphon in matins for the dead, Dirige, Domine, deus meus, in conspectu tuo viam meam.

senses.definition: The absence of harmony or concordance.

core.definition: A lack of agreement, balance, or peaceful relations among people, ideas, or parts of something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, HAR. Americans pronounce the r clearly, and the final -y becomes a long ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes conflict, tension, or clashing elements, and it is usually used in serious contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disharmony in writing and formal speech about families, teams, communities, or music and design. In everyday talk they more often say tension, conflict, or bad blood. Disharmony is a bit literary, so it sounds natural in a speech or an essay but a little stiff at a casual dinner.

distinctions.note: Discord is often more active or noisy, such as open quarrels or a dissonant chord; disharmony suggests a general lack of balance or agreement.
Conflict describes an open struggle between people or groups; disharmony can be quieter and refers to a broader lack of fit or peace.

examples.everyday: Things have felt a little disharmony at home since the move, so we're trying to talk more.
examples.professional: The team's disharmony showed up in missed deadlines and unanswered emails, so the manager called a retreat.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that disharmony between tradition and innovation is not simply a failure but a condition of creative life.

nuance.analogy: Disharmony is like an orchestra where every musician plays a different song: the sounds are there, but they no longer make music together.
nuance.etymology: From dis- (not, apart) and harmony, from Greek harmonia, joining or fitting together.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying dis-har-MO-ny instead of dis-HAR-muh-nee.
Using disharmony for a single argument; it describes a more general lack of agreement or balance.

senses.definition: An underground prison or vault, typically built underneath a castle.
The low area between two drumlins.
A shrewd person.
An area inhabited by enemies, containing story objectives, treasure, and bosses.
A room dedicated to sadomasochistic sexual activity.
To imprison in a dungeon.

core.definition: An underground prison cell, usually dark, damp, and in a castle or fortress.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The g is pronounced like the j in judge, and the last syllable is a weak uhn, so there is no separate ohn sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative and frightening. It evokes isolation, darkness, and suffering.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dungeon for medieval prisons, in fantasy novels and games, and in historical descriptions of castles. In modern American life, a jail cell or prison is the usual word for a real place of confinement. Calling a basement a dungeon is a playful exaggeration, often used jokingly.

distinctions.note: Prison is the general, modern word for a place where people are held; dungeon suggests an underground, medieval, and often grim cell.
A cellar is simply an underground storage room, while a dungeon is a place of confinement.

examples.everyday: We toured the old castle and saw the stone dungeon under the kitchen.
examples.professional: The game designer wants the dungeon levels to feel tense but not repetitive.
examples.analytical: The dungeon in the story stands for the isolation that the character feels inside his own mind.

nuance.analogy: A dungeon is like a locked storage closet for people: it is hidden, dark, and very hard to escape.
nuance.etymology: From Old French donjon, the main tower of a castle, from Latin dominio, lordship.
common_mistakes: Confusing dungeon with donjon, the main keep of a castle, which is a different structure.
Pronouncing the g as a hard g, as in DUN-gee-uhn.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, dungeon usually translates a Hebrew word for a prison or a pit used for confinement. Genesis 40:15 records Joseph's words that he was put in a pit or dungeon without reason, though in the RSV the word is more often rendered as prison in other places. Jeremiah 38:6 describes the prophet Jeremiah being lowered into a cistern or pit, a dungeon-like place, by his enemies. Jeremiah 37:16 mentions a dungeon cell where Jeremiah was kept for a long time.

dungeon.etymology: From Middle English *dongeoun* (“keep of a castle; dungeon; abyss, cave, den; whirlpool”), from Anglo-Norman *donjon* (“keep of a castle; keep used as a prison; dungeon”) and continental Old French *donjon* (“keep of a castle”), from Vulgar Latin…

senses.definition: Choose nutritious food; casual American usage (strictly, "eat healthily").

core.definition: To choose nutritious foods and eat in a way that supports good health.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HEL in healthy, and the final y is a light EE sound. Strictly, grammar calls for the adverb healthily, but Americans say healthy in casual speech, so you can use it in conversation.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests good habits and self-care, and it can sound slightly preachy if someone says it to others unasked.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this casually when talking about diet, such as with friends, family, or coworkers planning lunch. Strict grammar prefers eat healthily, which sounds more formal or written, so use it in essays or formal writing. A natural reply to someone saying they are trying to eat healthy is something like that's great, or good for you.

distinctions.note: Eat well can mean eating enough and enjoying food, not only choosing nutritious options.
Eat healthily is the grammatically standard adverb form and sounds more formal or written.

collocations: trying to eat healthy at work

examples.everyday: I'm trying to eat healthy this year, so I packed salad for lunch.
examples.professional: Our wellness team recommends that employees eat healthy during long travel days.
examples.analytical: Public health researchers often ask whether the phrase eat healthy has a clear meaning across different diets.

nuance.analogy: Like steering a car toward good roads, it means choosing the direction that keeps your body running well.
nuance.etymology: Healthy comes from Old English hǣlth, meaning wholeness or soundness.
common_mistakes: Using eat healthy in formal writing where eat healthily is expected.
Pronouncing the final y as a long I sound instead of EE.

conversation.text: I'm trying to eat healthy this year.
It's hard to eat healthy when you travel.
We eat healthy during the week and relax on weekends.

senses.definition: A pastoral poem, often in the form of a shepherd's monologue or a dialogue between shepherds.

core.definition: A short poem, usually pastoral, presented as a dialogue or monologue among shepherds or rural characters.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, EK. The final syllable is pronounced like 'og' in 'dog' in most American dialects, or like 'awg' in 'fog' for some speakers; the 'ue' is silent.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Eclogue is a term from literary history and classical studies, used in English departments, poetry courses and critical writing. Americans would never use it in everyday conversation. If discussing it in class, you might say 'a pastoral poem' to make the meaning clearer.

distinctions.note: Pastoral can mean a poem, painting or piece of music about rural life, while eclogue is specifically a poetic form in dialogue or monologue.
An idyll is a short poem or description of a peaceful, idealized scene, whereas an eclogue has a specific structure of shepherds speaking.

examples.everyday: My literature professor said that the poem I liked was actually an eclogue, a short conversation between two shepherds.
examples.professional: In the grant proposal, we cited Virgil's eclogues as an early model for pastoral writing in digital humanities projects.
examples.analytical: Spenser's eclogues use the convention of shepherd dialogue to address political and religious questions indirectly.

nuance.analogy: Like a short play set in a field, where the actors are shepherds talking about love, loss and the seasons.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ecloga, 'selection, extract', from Greek eklogē, 'selection', related to eclectic.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with the stress on the second syllable, as 'ek-LOG'.
Confusing it with epilogue, which is a closing section of a book or play.

eclogue.etymology: From Middle English *eclog*, from Latin *ecloga*, from Ancient Greek *ἐκλογή* (“selection”).

senses.definition: To instruct or train.
senses.example: Wang said such changes to the Baishui glacier provide the chance to educate visitors about global warming.

core.definition: To teach someone, especially in a school or formal setting, so they develop knowledge, skills and understanding.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EJ; the middle vowel is a reduced schwa, not oo. The d sounds like j, so say EJ-uh-kayt.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it can imply broad development of character, not just knowledge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use educate for schooling and broader learning, often in discussions of parents, schools, public health or training. In casual talk people more often say 'he went to school' or 'she's well read'. Educate is not used for a single lesson; use teach for that. A natural reply to 'Where were you educated?' is simply naming a school.

distinctions.note: Teach describes giving a lesson or showing how to do something; educate describes the broader process of developing knowledge and character over time.
Train focuses on specific skills for a job or activity; educate covers general knowledge and understanding.

examples.everyday: We're trying to educate our kids about money so they learn to budget before they turn eighteen.
examples.professional: Our data team tries to educate business partners on how model uncertainty affects their decisions.
examples.analytical: Plato argued that a just city must educate its citizens not only in facts but in virtue, shaping them toward the good.

nuance.analogy: Like tending a garden over years, not planting a single seed and walking away.
nuance.etymology: From Latin educare, to rear or bring up; often linked to educere, to lead out.
common_mistakes: Saying educate a lesson when you mean teach a lesson.
Pronouncing the middle vowel as a long oo, as in EJ-oo-kayt.
nuance.biblical_note: The Bible speaks of instruction and training rather than using the modern word educate. The Hebrew yasar carries the sense of discipline or instruction, as in Proverbs 22:6, which RSV renders as train up a child. The Greek paideuō means to train or educate, used in Ephesians 6:4 where fathers are told to bring up children in the discipline and instruction of the Lord, and 2 Timothy 3:16 speaks of scripture as useful for instruction in righteousness.

educate.etymology: From Middle English *educaten*, from *educat* + *-en*, from Latin *ēducātus*, the perfect passive participle of *ēducō* (“ to bring up, train, nourish; to rear, educate, train; to nourish, support, or produce”) (see *-ate*), further from an…

senses.definition: The linear subspace consisting of all eigenvectors associated with a particular eigenvalue, together with the zero vector.

core.definition: For a given eigenvalue, the set of all vectors that the matrix only scales by that eigenvalue, together with the zero vector.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, EYE. The 'space' part sounds like 'spays', with the vowel of 'day'. Do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; purely mathematical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eigenspace in linear algebra courses and research. It is sometimes called the eigenspace or eigenspace of a matrix, and it is always a vector subspace. Students often say 'the eigenspace for lambda equals two.'

distinctions.note: An eigenvector is a single nonzero vector; an eigenspace is the whole set of them for one eigenvalue, plus zero.
The null space is the eigenspace for eigenvalue zero, so it is a special case.

examples.everyday: My study partner says the eigenspace is basically all the vectors that stay on the same line.
examples.professional: The eigenspace for the largest eigenvalue captures most of the variance, so we keep only those directions.
examples.analytical: Since the eigenspace is a subspace, the sum of two eigenvectors with the same eigenvalue is again in the eigenspace.

nuance.analogy: An eigenspace is like a hallway where every person walks in the same direction: they may move faster or slower, but none of them turns.
nuance.etymology: From eigen, 'own', from German, and space, from Latin spatium, 'room'.
common_mistakes: Confusing eigenspace with eigenvector, which names only one direction.
Forgetting that the zero vector is included, so the eigenspace is always a subspace.

senses.definition: The act of making very lean.
The state of being emaciated or reduced to excessive leanness; an excessively lean condition.

core.definition: The state of being extremely thin and weak, usually from starvation or serious illness.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second -AY- syllable, and the 'ci' sounds like 'sh'. The ending is 'shun', not 'shee-un'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a serious medical or humanitarian condition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use emaciation in medical, nutritional, and humanitarian writing, such as reports on famine or illness. In everyday talk, people say 'severe weight loss' or 'wasting away'. It is a precise clinical noun, so use it when you want a formal, serious description.

distinctions.note: Malnutrition names the cause, a lack of proper nutrition; emaciation names the visible result of extreme weight loss.
Starvation describes the lack of food itself; emaciation describes the body's physical wasting that can follow.

examples.everyday: The doctor said his weight loss and emaciation meant he needed to be admitted right away.
examples.professional: The relief report documented signs of emaciation among children in the camp.
examples.analytical: The essay treats emaciation not only as a biological state but as a symbol of social neglect.

nuance.analogy: Emaciation is like a river drying up to a thin trickle, with only the riverbed left behind.
nuance.etymology: From Latin emaciatio, from emaciare 'to make lean', from macer 'lean'.
common_mistakes: Confusing emaciation with emancipation, which is a different word meaning freedom.
Using emaciation casually for ordinary thinness.

senses.definition: In AI: The part of a model that turns the input into an internal representation, such as a vector of numbers.
A device or algorithm used to encode something.
A sensor which converts a position into an electronic signal.

core.definition: In AI, the part of a model that converts an input, such as text or an image, into a compact internal representation made of numbers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KOH, the second syllable. The final -er is a reduced rhotic vowel, so say 'dur' and not 'dehr' or 'dayr'.

nuance.connotation: neutral; it is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: In American data science and machine learning teams, encoder almost always means the AI component unless the context is hardware. A rotary encoder is a sensor, so listen for the context. Engineers say 'the encoder' casually in meetings, and they expect a listener to know which kind is meant.

distinctions.note: An encoder turns input into a representation, while a decoder turns that representation back into an output.
An embedding is the vector an encoder produces, while the encoder is the whole component that creates it.

examples.everyday: My cousin works on speech software, and she says their encoder turns each voice clip into a short list of numbers.
examples.professional: The encoder compresses each customer record into a 256-dimensional vector before the classifier runs.
examples.analytical: The encoder maps raw input into a latent space in which similar inputs lie close together, which is why its representations transfer well to other tasks.

nuance.analogy: Like a translator who writes a private shorthand summary that only the team can read, the encoder compresses the input into its own compact code.
nuance.etymology: From 'encode' (en- plus code), with 'code' from Latin 'codex' (a block of wood or a book).
common_mistakes: Using 'encoder' for the whole model; it is only one part of it.
Confusing an encoder with a decoder, which reverses the process.

conversation.text: The encoder turns the input into a representation that the rest of the model can use.
We'll use a pretrained text encoder and train only a small classification head.
The one-hot encoder maps each category to its own binary column.

senses.definition: To enhance.
To make (someone or something) rich or richer.
senses.example: Hobbies enrich lives.

senses.definition: To adorn, ornate more richly.
To add nutrients or fertilizer to the soil; to fertilize.
To add nutrients to foodstuffs; to fortify.
To increase the amount of one isotope in a mixture of isotopes, especially in a nuclear fuel.
To make to rise the proportion of a given constituent.

core.definition: To improve something by adding quality, value or substance, or to make someone wealthier.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable 'rich', and the vowel is a short i, as in 'sit'. Do not stretch it into 'in-REECH'; the ch sounds like the ch in 'church'.

nuance.connotation: positive: it describes improving or deepening something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use enrich for food, education, culture and relationships, as in 'enrich your life' or 'enriched flour'. Enriched on a label means nutrients were added back. Enrich yourself is a negative way of saying someone is gaining money unfairly.

distinctions.note: Enhance means make something better or more attractive, while enrich suggests adding depth or valuable content.
Improve is the general word; enrich suggests adding something valuable to the existing thing.
Fortify means add strength or nutrients, and it is common for food, while enrich covers quality more broadly.

examples.everyday: This recipe calls for a splash of cream to enrich the sauce.
examples.professional: Mentoring new hires really enriches the knowledge base of our whole team.
examples.analytical: Hermeneutical debate can enrich interpretation by bringing forward readings that the tradition neglected.

nuance.analogy: Like adding compost to tired soil so that it can support more growth.
nuance.etymology: From Old French enrichir, from en- plus riche, rich.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it in-REECH with a long e.
Using enrich only for money, when it often refers to quality, value or nutrition.

enrich.etymology: From Middle English *enrichen*, from Anglo-Norman *enrichir* and Old French *enrichier*.

senses.definition: The repetition of the same word or clause after intervening matter.

core.definition: A figure of speech that repeats a word or phrase from the start of a clause at its end, with other words in between.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LEP, the third syllable. The other syllables are reduced to 'uh' sounds, so do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: neutral; it names a rhetorical device, so praising a speech's epanalepsis signals good writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in English classes, literary criticism, and talk about speeches, rarely in casual conversation. A teacher might say 'the poet uses epanalepsis to bring the image back at the close.' At a dinner table, say 'repetition' or 'echo' instead.

distinctions.note: Anaphora repeats the same word at the start of successive clauses; epanalepsis repeats the opening word at the end of a clause.
Epistrophe repeats a word at the end of successive clauses, while epanalepsis links the end of one clause back to its beginning.

examples.everyday: Dad, you're doing that epanalepsis thing again, starting and ending with 'I'm fine.'
examples.professional: In the keynote, the speaker used epanalepsis to end on the word 'listen', which made the close memorable.
examples.analytical: The poem's epanalepsis returns to 'grace' at the close of the stanza, framing the argument around God's initiative.

nuance.analogy: Like a bookend: the same word stands at both ends of a clause and holds the middle in place.
nuance.etymology: From Greek epanalēpsis, 'a taking up again', from epi- 'upon' and analambanein 'to take up again'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable; the main stress is on LEP.
Confusing it with anaphora; epanalepsis repeats the opening word at the end, not at the start of each clause.

epanalepsis.etymology: Latin *epanalepsis*, from Ancient Greek *ἐπανάληψις*, from *ἐπαναλαμβάνω*, from *ἐπί* + *ἀνά* + *λαμβάνω*.

senses.definition: Of, from, or pertaining to, Ephesus.
Someone from Ephesus.
A jolly companion; a roisterer.

core.definition: A New Testament letter traditionally attributed to Paul, written to Christians in the region of Ephesus, about God's grace, the unity of the church and living a new life.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on FEE, the second syllable, and the -sians ending is pronounced like the s in vision, so it sounds like zhunz. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or pronounce the ph as p, so use the f sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in religious settings, where the letter is widely quoted for its teaching on grace and the church.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Ephesians mostly in church, Bible study, sermons and religious conversation. People often say the book of Ephesians or refer to a verse like Ephesians 2:8, and they may shorten it to Ephesians in casual talk. It is a common reference in weddings, where Ephesians 5 is often read.

distinctions.note: Ephesus is the ancient city in western Asia Minor, while Ephesians is the New Testament letter addressed to Christians in or near that region.
Galatians is another Pauline letter focused on freedom from the law, while Ephesians emphasizes the unity of the church and the believer's life in Christ.

examples.everyday: I'm reading Ephesians tonight because the part about grace helps me this week.
examples.professional: Our ministry newsletter quotes Ephesians 4 whenever we talk about working together across different teams.
examples.analytical: Ephesians presents the church as Christ's body, grounding ethical instruction in the believer's new identity.

nuance.analogy: Ephesians is like a blueprint that shows how a building fits together, with grace as the foundation and the church as the finished structure.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin Epistola ad Ephesios, letter to the Ephesians, from Ephesus, the city in western Asia Minor.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in EF-eh-zee-unz, instead of FEE.
Pronouncing the ending as -zee-unz, which is acceptable in some speech but not the most common American form.
Confusing Ephesians with Ephesus, which is the city rather than the letter.
nuance.biblical_note: Ephesians is a New Testament letter in the Pauline tradition, traditionally attributed to Paul, although many scholars today question whether Paul wrote it. Key Greek words include charis, grace, and ekklesia, church or assembly. Ephesians 2:8-9 teaches that salvation comes by grace through faith and not by works, a central Protestant text on justification. Ephesians 4:4-6 stresses the unity of the one body, one Spirit and one hope. Ephesians 6:10-18 uses the image of the armor of God to describe spiritual conflict.

senses.definition: Containing an error; inaccurate.
senses.example: His answer to the sum was erroneous.

senses.definition: Derived from an error.
senses.example: His conclusion was erroneous, since it was based on a false assumption.

senses.definition: Mistaken.
senses.example: Her choice at the line-up proved to be erroneous, as she had only seen the mugger for an instant.

senses.definition: Deviating from the requirements of the law, but without a lack of legal authority, thus not illegal.
senses.example: If, while having the power to act, one commits error in the exercise of that power, he acts erroneously.

core.definition: Incorrect or mistaken, especially a fact, belief, number, or claim that is wrong because of an error.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ROH, the second syllable. The first syllable is a reduced schwa, and the last syllable is 'us', not 'ous' as in 'famous'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies that something is factually wrong, but it is more neutral than calling someone a liar.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use erroneous in formal writing, news, legal and academic contexts, and business reports to describe wrong information or conclusions. In casual speech people say 'wrong' or 'not right.' Calling a claim erroneous is a polite way to say it is incorrect without accusing anyone.

distinctions.note: Wrong is the everyday, general word, while erroneous is more formal and specifically implies a mistake in facts or information.
Mistaken usually describes a person's belief or judgment, while erroneous describes the thing itself, such as a figure, report, or assumption.

examples.everyday: The website showed an erroneous price, so the cashier had to correct it before I paid.
examples.professional: The dashboard showed erroneous sales figures because one data feed was double-counting orders.
examples.analytical: The argument rests on an erroneous assumption that correlation always indicates causation.

nuance.analogy: An erroneous claim is like a map with a wrong road drawn on it: the mistake is in the source, so everyone who follows it goes astray.
nuance.etymology: From Latin erroneus, meaning wandering, from errare, to wander.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as ER-uh-nee-us.
Saying 'ER-oh-nee-ous' with an extra syllable at the end.
Using erroneous for a person; it describes information or conclusions, while a person is more often described as mistaken.

erroneous.etymology: From late Middle English *erroneous*, from Middle French *erroneux*, from Latin *erroneus*.

senses.definition: An inauthentic or inadequate substitute or imitation.
senses.example: Back then, we could only get ersatz coffee.

senses.definition: Something made in imitation; an effigy or substitute.

core.definition: Made as a cheaper, inferior substitute for something genuine; artificial or fake.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the middle sound a voiced z, not an s. The final 'ts' is a short, sharp sound, and the last vowel is the open 'ah' of American 'cot' because of the cot-caught merger.

nuance.connotation: negative, because it implies something is a poor imitation of something better.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ersatz' mostly to describe fake or substitute products, like ersatz coffee or ersatz leather, or in discussions of culture where something feels inauthentic. It is more common in writing and in conversation with educated speakers than in casual talk. Calling something ersatz is a mild insult, so use it carefully when speaking about people's work or food you are served.

distinctions.note: Fake implies deliberate deception; ersatz implies a deliberate substitute that is inferior but not necessarily meant to deceive.
Artificial is neutral and describes something made by people; ersatz adds a judgment that the imitation is poor.

examples.everyday: That 'cheese' on the pizza tastes like ersatz plastic, honestly.
examples.professional: The vendor's demo was an ersatz version of the dashboard, with the real data pipeline left out.
examples.analytical: Critics argued that the festival offered an ersatz authenticity, a staged folk culture designed for tourists.

nuance.analogy: Like a plastic plant in a room: it fills the space and looks like the real thing from across the room, but up close you know it is not alive.
nuance.etymology: From German Ersatz, 'replacement', from ersetzen, 'to replace'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'ur-SAHTS' with a rhotic first vowel and the stress on the second syllable; the stress is on the first syllable.
Using it as a neutral word for any substitute, when it carries a negative judgment about quality.

senses.definition: To marry.
To accept, support, or take on as one’s own (an idea or a cause).

core.definition: To publicly adopt, support, or champion an idea, belief, or cause as your own.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable and end with a voiced z sound, not an s. The first vowel is a short reduced ih, not ee.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests a deliberate, public commitment to a position, often a political, social, or philosophical one.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use espouse mainly in writing and formal speech, such as news reports, essays, and debates about public policy. In casual talk they would say support, back, or believe in. The verb's old sense of marrying is archaic in American English, so avoid it in modern conversation.

distinctions.note: Support is everyday and can mean simply helping someone. Espouse implies a formal, deliberate adoption of a belief or cause.
Advocate suggests actively arguing for something in public. Espouse focuses on holding and declaring a view as your own, not necessarily campaigning for it.

examples.everyday: My brother has started espousing a lot of strange diet theories, and it's driving my mom crazy.
examples.professional: In the planning meeting, the director espoused a data-first approach to every new product launch.
examples.analytical: Locke espouses a view of personal identity grounded in continuous consciousness rather than in the substance of the soul.

nuance.analogy: Like planting a flag on a belief and saying publicly, this is mine.
nuance.etymology: From Old French espouser, from Latin sponsare, from spondere 'to promise'.
common_mistakes: Using espouse for everyday support, as in 'I espouse you' for 'I support you'; it sounds stiff or confusing.
Confusing it with expouse or expose; the stress and meaning are different.
Using the archaic sense 'to marry' in modern American speech.

espouse.etymology: From Middle English *espousen*, borrowed from Old French *espouser*, from Latin *spōnsō* (frequentative of *spondeō*), from Proto-Indo-European **spend-*.

senses.definition: Feeling great well-being or elation or intense happiness; characterized by euphoria.
senses.example: In this moment, I am euphoric.

senses.definition: Productive of euphoria, causing great joy.
A drug that causes euphoria; a euphoriant.

core.definition: Feeling intense joy, excitement or well-being; also, causing such a feeling.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FOR, the second syllable. Pronounce the r clearly, and keep the final -ic as a short 'ik' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive, describing joy. It can be used humorously or with a hint of excess, especially about drugs or a crowd's mood.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use euphoric to describe a strong mood after an exciting event, like a victory or a long-awaited announcement. In everyday talk people might say 'over the moon' or 'so happy.' The noun form, meaning a drug that causes euphoria, is used in medical or drug-policy discussions.

distinctions.note: Ecstatic is stronger and more emotional, often suggesting overwhelming delight; euphoric suggests a lighter, more elated feeling.
Happy is general and calm; euphoric describes an intense, sometimes temporary high.

examples.everyday: We were euphoric after the game, and nobody could stop smiling.
examples.professional: The client was euphoric about the results, so we agreed to schedule the rollout for next quarter.
examples.analytical: Whitehead warns that euphoric certainty about progress can blind a culture to the costs of its own success.

nuance.analogy: Like a balloon that has been filled to the top, so light and full that it seems to float.
nuance.etymology: From euphoria, with the adjective ending -ic, from Greek euphoria.
common_mistakes: Using 'euphoric' for mild satisfaction, which overstates the feeling.
Stressing the first syllable, saying 'YOO-fo-ric.'

senses.definition: To a great or unusual degree, extent, etc. extremely.

core.definition: To an extremely great or unusual degree; very or extremely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the second syllable, 'seed.' The final -ly is a light 'lee,' and the middle 'ing' is a short, quick vowel, so do not stretch it into 'ee-ing'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it intensifies a quality and can sound slightly elevated or old-fashioned in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exceedingly mostly in writing and formal speech, such as reports, essays, or sermons. In everyday conversation, people say 'very' or 'extremely' instead. Using it in a casual chat can sound stiff, though it is natural in a formal letter or toast.

distinctions.note: Very is the everyday, neutral intensifier, while exceedingly is more formal and emphatic.
Extremely is common in speech and writing; exceedingly sounds more literary and old-fashioned.

examples.everyday: At the wedding toast, my uncle said he was exceedingly grateful to have us all there.
examples.professional: The new vendor's delivery times were exceedingly unreliable, so we switched suppliers.
examples.analytical: The argument is exceedingly subtle, because it depends on distinguishing two senses of 'cause' that the author never separates.

nuance.analogy: Like turning a dial all the way up past the usual marks.
nuance.etymology: From exceeding (present participle of exceed) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'exceedingly' in casual conversation where 'very' sounds more natural.
Mispronouncing the middle syllables as 'ex-SEE-dee-ing-lee' instead of 'ik-SEE-ding-lee'.

senses.definition: The quality of being excellent; brilliance.
senses.example: John Davies was awarded for excellence in the field of computer security.

senses.definition: Something in which one excels.
An excellent or valuable quality; something at which any someone excels; a virtue.

core.definition: The quality of being exceptionally good; outstanding skill, quality, or achievement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, 'EK.' The second and third syllables are reduced to a quick 'suh' and 'lunss,' so do not give each syllable equal weight.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it signals high standards and admiration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use excellence in schools, workplaces, and mission statements, as in 'a commitment to excellence.' It can sound formal or slogan-like in casual talk. In everyday speech, people more often say 'really good' or 'top quality.'

distinctions.note: Quality is a neutral word for how good something is, while excellence means a very high degree of quality.
Perfection means having no flaws at all, while excellence means being outstanding even if flaws remain.

examples.everyday: The bakery down the street has a reputation for excellence, so we always order from there for birthdays.
examples.professional: Our team is committed to excellence in every release we ship to customers.
examples.analytical: For Aquinas, the virtues are dispositions toward excellence in human action, not merely useful habits.

nuance.analogy: Like a top athlete whose skill stands far above the crowd.
nuance.etymology: From Latin excellentia, from excellens, 'surpassing, eminent,' from excellere.
common_mistakes: Using 'excellence' as a verb; the verb is 'excel.'
Using the plural 'excellences' in ordinary speech, where it is rare.

excellence.etymology: From Middle English *excellence*, from Old French *excellence*, from Latin *excellentia*.

senses.definition: The number by which a value (called the base) is said to be raised to a power in exponentiation: for example, the 3 in 23=8.
One who expounds, represents or advocates.
A phonological manifestation of a morphosyntactic property; in layman's terms, the expression of one or more grammatical properties by sound.
The part of a floating-point number that represents its exponent value.

core.definition: A small number written above and to the right of a value to show how many times it is multiplied by itself.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SPOH. The final syllable is reduced to 'nunt', not 'nent'. Do not say it like 'opponent' with a different stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in math; in the sense 'advocate' it is formal and positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'two to the third power' or 'two cubed' as well as 'two to the exponent three', but in school math 'exponent' is the small number. The sense 'advocate' is formal and often appears in academic or policy writing; Americans more often say 'proponent' or 'advocate'.

distinctions.note: Power can mean the whole expression, as in 2 to the power of 3, while exponent names the small number, 3.
The base is the number being multiplied; the exponent is the number that says how many times.

examples.everyday: My daughter asked what the little number above the 2 means, so I told her it's an exponent.
examples.professional: The exponent in the growth formula is wrong, so the forecast doubles every year instead of every ten.
examples.analytical: Writing the exponent as a variable lets us express the relation between growth rate and time as a continuous function.

nuance.analogy: The exponent is like an instruction on a recipe telling you how many times to stack the base ingredient on itself.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exponere, 'to put forth, set out'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'expo-NENT' with the stress on the last syllable.
Confusing the math sense with the rarer sense 'advocate', which is 'exponent' in formal writing.

exponent.etymology: From Latin *expōnēns*, of *expōnō* (“to expose; to exhibit, display, set out; to explain”), from *ex-* + *pōnō*.

senses.definition: A group of people, especially within a political organization, which expresses a shared belief or opinion different from people who are not part of the group.
Strife; discord.
A form of literature, film etc. that treats real people or events as if they were fiction; a mix of fact and fiction.
The facts found in fiction.

core.definition: A small group within a larger organization, especially a political party, that holds its own views and often works against the main leadership.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, FAK. The ending '-tion' is pronounced 'shun', with a reduced final vowel, not as a separate 'tee-on'.

nuance.connotation: often negative; it suggests division or disloyalty, though it can be neutral when describing legitimate internal groups.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'faction' mostly in news and political discussion, such as 'a conservative faction of the party'. It usually implies a group that is somewhat at odds with the main body. In casual talk people often say 'wing' or 'side' instead, so 'faction' sounds slightly formal and analytical.

distinctions.note: 'Wing' is informal and common in US politics; 'faction' is more formal and emphasizes division.
A party is a whole organization; a faction is a subgroup inside it that often has its own agenda.
A clique is a small, exclusive social group; a faction is a political or organizational group with shared aims.

examples.everyday: My uncle says there's a whole faction in his church that won't agree to any change.
examples.professional: The product team split into two factions, one wanting a rapid release and the other wanting more testing.
examples.analytical: Madison's account of the republic treats faction as an unavoidable product of human nature and liberty.

nuance.analogy: A faction is like a team of rowers in one boat who start pulling in different directions.
nuance.etymology: From Latin factio, 'a making, a party', from facere, 'to make or do'.
common_mistakes: Using 'faction' to mean 'fiction' or a made-up story.
Saying 'a faction of people' when 'a faction' already means a group of people.

faction.etymology: Middle French *faction*, from Latin *factiō* (“a group of people acting together, a political faction”), noun of process from perfect passive participle *factus*, from *faciō* (“do, make”).

senses.definition: So as to produce a fine texture; into small, thin, or delicate pieces.
senses.example: Fledglings can only be fed finely chopped meat.

senses.definition: In a fine, handsome or attractive way; very well.

core.definition: Into very small, thin, or delicate pieces, or with great precision and care.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. Keep the long i and the n clear, and make the final syllable a light 'lee' sound.

nuance.connotation: positive
nuance.usage_note: In American cooking, finely is common in recipes ('finely chopped onion'), and it is also used in product descriptions and reviews. For a more casual meaning, Americans say 'really well' or 'perfectly.' It is neutral and clear in almost any setting.

distinctions.note: Roughly means in a rough or approximate way, while finely means in small, precise pieces or with detail.
Thinly means in thin layers or slices, while finely refers to small particles or detailed texture.

examples.everyday: Chop the garlic finely so it melts into the sauce instead of burning in the pan.
examples.professional: The model's parameters are finely tuned to our fraud data, so it should not be used for other products.
examples.analytical: The argument is finely balanced between two competing readings of the text, and neither side clearly wins.

nuance.analogy: Finely is like a sieve turned to its smallest holes: whatever goes through is small, even and carefully separated.
nuance.etymology: From fine (from Old French fin, from Latin finis) plus -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing finely with 'fine' as an adverb in everyday speech; 'finely' is the correct adverb for chopping and tuning.
Using finely to mean quickly or easily; it refers to small, precise, or detailed qualities.

senses.definition: The phenomenon in which a data-gathering instrument has a lower limit to the data values it can reliably specify.

core.definition: A measurement limit where scores cannot go below a minimum, so many people cluster at the lowest possible score.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word. Floor is rhotic, with a clear r and the vowel of more. Effect has a short eh in the stressed syllable, so do not say ih-FECT with a flat vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral technical term; it describes a limit of measurement rather than a person's outcome.
nuance.usage_note: Researchers say a test has a floor effect when many participants score at the bottom, so the test cannot show improvement or differences at the low end. The opposite is a ceiling effect. Americans use the term in psychology, education and survey research.

distinctions.note: A ceiling effect occurs when many scores pile up at the maximum; a floor effect piles up at the minimum.
Range restriction is the broader problem of a narrow spread of scores; a floor effect is a specific case where the lowest values are clipped.

examples.everyday: My teacher said the quiz had a floor effect, since almost everyone scored zero.
examples.professional: The survey shows a floor effect on the satisfaction item, so we need a lower-level question to tell customers apart.
examples.analytical: A floor effect means the instrument cannot register differences below its lower limit, so true variation among the lowest scorers is hidden.

nuance.analogy: Like a bathroom scale that reads zero for anyone under a certain weight: you cannot tell how light they are.
nuance.etymology: English floor (lowest level) plus effect (result), used in measurement research.
common_mistakes: Using floor problem instead of the standard term floor effect.
Using floor effect as an everyday phrase for being on the ground.

senses.definition: The elements of an image which lie closest to the picture plane.
The subject of an image, often depicted at the bottom in a two-dimensional work.
The application the user is currently interacting with; the application window that appears in front of all others.
To place in the foreground (physically or metaphorically).

core.definition: The part of an image, scene, or screen that appears closest to the viewer, or the area where the main action or focus is.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FOR, and let the second syllable be lighter. The 'ground' part rhymes with 'sound', and the r in 'fore' should be strongly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes position or focus and carries no positive or negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'foreground' is used in art, photography, film, and software. The sense of 'the application you are using now' is common in computer talk. For a metaphorical use, Americans often say 'bring to the foreground' or 'keep in the foreground'.

distinctions.note: 'Background' is the part farthest from the viewer, while 'foreground' is the closest part of the image or scene.
'Front' describes the part facing forward in general, while 'foreground' is specific to pictures, scenes, or the main focus of attention.

examples.everyday: In that photo, my dog is in the foreground and the mountains are way back in the distance.
examples.professional: Please move the chart to the foreground so the team can see the key metrics before the meeting starts.
examples.analytical: The painter places the human figure in the foreground, which makes the landscape seem to recede into a symbolic background.

nuance.analogy: The foreground is like the front row at a concert: it is closest to you and gets most of your attention.
nuance.etymology: From 'fore' (in front) plus 'ground' (the base or surface).
common_mistakes: Confusing 'foreground' with 'background' when describing a picture.
Using 'in front' for everything; 'foreground' suggests a particular visual or focus area.

senses.definition: Able to be foreseen or anticipated.
senses.example: This project will not be finished in the foreseeable future.

core.definition: Able to be predicted or expected in advance, based on what is known now.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEE. The second syllable is a quick, reduced 'uh', and the final syllable is a light 'buhl'. Americans often say the whole word in about three beats.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is common in business, legal, and technical writing, where it signals that a risk or result could reasonably be expected.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'foreseeable' a lot in contracts, insurance, law, and project planning, often in phrases like 'in the foreseeable future'. In casual talk, people say 'soon' or 'in the near future'. A natural reply is simply 'Got it' or 'Sounds good'.

distinctions.note: 'Predictable' describes something that happens in a regular or expected way; 'foreseeable' focuses on what could be known in advance, often in a legal or planning sense.
'Unforeseen' means that something was not expected; 'foreseeable' means it could have been expected.

examples.everyday: We won't be moving to a bigger house in the foreseeable future, so we'll stay put.
examples.professional: The contract covers all foreseeable risks, but it does not include the rare events listed in the appendix.
examples.analytical: A moral agent is responsible only for the foreseeable consequences of an action, not for every effect that follows from it.

nuance.analogy: Like a weather forecast that shows rain on the horizon: the storm is foreseeable before it arrives.
nuance.etymology: From 'foresee' plus the suffix '-able'.
common_mistakes: Using 'foreseeable' for things that are already known, rather than things that can be expected.
Pronouncing the middle syllables too strongly; they should be quick and light.

senses.definition: The act, process, or result of formulating or reducing to a formula.
senses.example: The formulation with the bare infinitive was somewhat less common.

senses.definition: A particular linguistic construction; a turn of phrase.
senses.example: The formulation with the bare infinitive was somewhat less common.

senses.definition: A medicinal preparation.
senses.example: If you liked our old shampoo, you'll love the new kinder, gentler formulation.

core.definition: A clear, precise statement or wording of an idea, plan, or principle.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on LAY, the third syllable. The first syllable is a secondary stress, and the final shun is weak, so do not stress the ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests careful, precise thinking, though it can sound jargon-heavy in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use formulation in professional, academic, and scientific settings, as in 'The formulation of the policy needs work.' In pharmaceuticals and cosmetics, it means a specific mix of ingredients. In everyday talk they usually say 'wording' or 'way of putting it'.

distinctions.note: Wording is the exact choice of words, while formulation is the broader act or result of stating an idea precisely.
Formula is a set expression or mathematical rule, while formulation is the process or result of creating that expression.

examples.everyday: The new formulation of this lotion is less greasy, so I like it better.
examples.professional: The team agreed on a new formulation of the feature request, which cut the scope in half.
examples.analytical: Rawls's formulation of the difference principle has been challenged by critics who doubt its ordering of liberties.

nuance.analogy: A good formulation is like a well-cut key: it fits the lock of an idea exactly and opens the right door.
nuance.etymology: From formulate, from Latin formula, a rule or small form.
common_mistakes: Using it for a casual phrase; 'wording' or 'phrasing' is more natural.
Mispronouncing the stress as 'FAWR-myuh-lay-shun' with the primary on FOR instead of LAY.

senses.definition: From the very beginning; from the outset; immediately upon starting.
senses.example: I watched him closely from the get-go because I did not trust him.

core.definition: From the very beginning; right from the start of something.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on "go" in "get-go," with a secondary stress on "get." Say "thuh" with a reduced vowel, and link the words smoothly in speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly positive. It emphasizes an immediate, clear starting point, sometimes with the implication that something was always true.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "from the get-go" in casual conversation and work talk to mean from the very beginning. It is informal but widely used by adults in offices and everyday life. A natural reply is "Yeah, I knew that from the get-go" or "It was clear from the get-go."

distinctions.note: From the start is neutral and widely used; from the get-go is more colloquial and emphatic.
From the outset is more formal, often used in writing or serious business contexts.

collocations: it was clear from the get-go
I knew that from the get-go

examples.everyday: I knew this movie wasn't for me from the get-go.
examples.professional: The client had concerns about the timeline from the get-go, so we planned for them early.
examples.analytical: The argument's weakness was evident from the get-go, since its first premise assumes what it sets out to prove.

nuance.analogy: From the get-go is like the starting gun in a race: it sets the pace from the very first step.
common_mistakes: Saying "from the get go" without the hyphen in writing; the standard written form is "from the get-go."
Using it in very formal writing, where "from the outset" fits better.

conversation.text: I liked her from the get-go.
The project had problems from the get-go.
We should have involved legal from the get-go.

senses.definition: A utensil in the shape of an inverted hollow cone terminating in a narrow pipe, for channeling liquids or granular material; typically used when transferring said substances from any container into ones with a significantly smaller opening.
A passage or avenue for a fluid or flowing substance; specifically, a smoke flue or pipe; the chimney of a steamship or the like.
Ellipsis of purchase funnel (“the process of customer acquisition conceptualized as a series of stages, from initial awareness (top) to sale or conversion (bottom)”).
senses.example: top of (the) funnel marketing

senses.definition: Ellipsis of funnel cloud.
To use a funnel.
To proceed through a narrow gap or passageway akin to a funnel; to condense or narrow.
senses.example: Expect delays where the traffic funnels down to one lane.

senses.definition: To channel, direct, or focus (emotions, money, resources, etc.).
senses.example: Our taxes are being funneled into pointless government initiatives.

senses.definition: To consume (beer, etc.) rapidly through a funnel, typically as a stunt at a party.

core.definition: A cone-shaped tool with a narrow tube at the bottom, used to pour liquid or powder into a container with a small opening.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FUN. The final -el is a syllabic l with no vowel, so say it as 'FUN-l' and avoid adding an extra 'uh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word, and the verb and figurative senses are also neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use funnel for kitchen tools and car fluids, and in everyday talk, such as 'Hold the funnel while I pour the oil.' In marketing and data science, 'funnel' refers to the stages a customer passes through, such as awareness, interest, and purchase, often called a purchase funnel or sales funnel. In the verb sense, Americans say 'funnel money into' or 'funnel people through' a process.

distinctions.note: A funnel guides liquid into a container; a strainer separates solids from liquid.
Pour is the action of moving liquid; a funnel is the tool that makes the pouring more accurate.

examples.everyday: Hold the funnel steady so the oil doesn't spill all over the engine.
examples.professional: Marketing wants to funnel more leads into the trial sign-up page, so we need to track drop-off at each stage.
examples.analytical: Bayesian updating can be pictured as a funnel that narrows the range of plausible hypotheses as evidence accumulates.

nuance.analogy: A funnel is like a narrow gate on a busy road, forcing many cars to pass through one lane.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin fundella, from Latin fundere, 'to pour'.
common_mistakes: Saying /ˈfʌnl/ with an extra vowel, or stressing the second syllable.
Using 'funnel' for a strainer or colander, which separates solids from liquids.

funnel.etymology: From Middle English *funell*, *fonel*, probably through Old French **founel* (compare, *enfounilh*), from Latin *fundibulum*, *infundibulum* (“funnel”), from *infundere* (“to pour in”)

senses.definition: In the Bible, a son of Jacob and Zilpah, ancestor of the tribe of Gad, and also a prophet who advised King David.

core.definition: In the Bible, a son of Jacob and Zilpah, ancestor of the tribe of Gad, and also a prophet who advised King David.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it with a short a, as in 'bad,' and a hard g, as in 'go.' Do not confuse it with 'god' or with the verb 'gad about.'

nuance.connotation: neutral; a name from Scripture with no negative or positive shift in ordinary use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often meet this name in Bible study, Sunday school or Christian reading. Outside religious contexts the name is rare. Its familiar verb use, as in 'gad about' (to wander around restlessly), is a separate word with a different spelling of meaning and is informal.

distinctions.note: Gad is the person or the tribe's name; Gadite refers to a member of the tribe of Gad.
This is an informal phrasal verb meaning to travel or wander around for pleasure, not the biblical name.

collocations: Gad's territory east of the Jordan

examples.everyday: We're reading about Gad in Bible study on Wednesday, so I need to look up who he was.
examples.professional: In my lesson on the twelve tribes, I give students a short chart showing where Gad settled and how Gad's role differs from Gad the prophet.
examples.analytical: The name Gad in Genesis 30:11 is tied to the Hebrew word for fortune, and the blessings on the tribe in Deuteronomy 33 reveal how the tribe was understood in Israel's self-identity.

nuance.analogy: Like a family name shared by a founder and a clan, Gad names both the ancestor and the group descended from him.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew gad, 'fortune' or 'troop,' the name given to Jacob's son in Genesis 30:11.
common_mistakes: Saying 'god' instead of Gad, which changes the name's pronunciation and meaning.
Using 'Gad' as a separate noun for the tribe when Americans say 'the tribe of Gad' or 'the Gadites.'
nuance.biblical_note: Gad was the seventh son of Jacob, born to Zilpah, Leah's servant (Genesis 30:11). The tribe of Gad received land east of the Jordan (Numbers 32:1-5, where Gad and Reuben ask Moses for land there). Gad is also a prophet who served David as seer (1 Samuel 22:5; 2 Samuel 24:11-14). The Hebrew word gad means 'fortune' or 'troop,' which links the name to Isaiah 65:11, where the RSV uses 'Fortune' for a pagan deity.

senses.definition: To open the mouth wide, especially involuntarily, as in a yawn, anger, or surprise.
To stare in wonder.
To open wide; to display a gap.
senses.example: The wound was gaping open and losing too much blood.

senses.definition: To open the passage to the vomeronasal organ, analogous to the flehming in other animals.
To depict a dilated anal or vaginal cavity upon penetrative sexual activity.
A large opening.
A disease in poultry caused by gapeworm in the windpipe, a symptom of which is frequent gaping.
The width of an opening.
The maximum opening of the mouth (of a bird, fish, etc.) when it is open.
An act of gaping; a yawn.

core.definition: To open the mouth wide, often in surprise, or to stare in wonder or amazement at something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the one syllable and make a long a glide to a p sound. Do not confuse it with gap, which has a short a.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. Gaping at someone can seem rude, while gaping in wonder can be positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gape when someone stares open-mouthed in surprise or shock, as in people gaped at the accident. Saying someone is gaping at you may sound rude. In everyday speech, stare or gawk is more common, and gape is more descriptive or literary.

distinctions.note: Stare means to look fixedly for a long time, while gape adds the image of an open mouth from surprise or amazement.
Gawk is informal and suggests rude or foolish staring, while gape is more neutral and can describe any surprise.

examples.everyday: When the waiter brought out the giant dessert, the whole table gaped at it in surprise.
examples.professional: The new dashboard was so complicated that the executives gaped at the screen and asked for a simpler version.
examples.analytical: The prophetic text uses the image of enemies opening their mouths wide to show the depth of hostility and the vulnerability of the speaker.

nuance.analogy: Gape is like a door that swings open suddenly, leaving a wide space you cannot ignore.
nuance.etymology: From Old English gapian, meaning to open the mouth wide.
common_mistakes: Confusing gape with gap, which is a noun or a space between things.
Saying gape at someone in a casual conversation, which can sound rude.
Using gape for simple looking; it implies surprise or openness.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Psalms and Lamentations, the image of enemies opening their mouths wide expresses hostility and threat. The RSV describes enemies gaping at the afflicted speaker. Psalm 22:13 describes enemies opening their mouths like a roaring lion. Lamentations 2:16 describes enemies opening their mouths wide against Jerusalem, showing scorn and triumph over the fallen city.

gape.etymology: From Middle English *gapen*, from Old Norse *gapa* (“to gape”), perhaps.

senses.definition: A cuckoo; any gawky bird.
A fool; a simpleton; a stupid or clumsy person.
A conspicuous or stupid stare or gape; an instance of gawking.
To stare or gape stupidly.
To stare conspicuously.
To suck.

core.definition: To stare openly and rudely, often with your mouth partly open, usually because you are surprised or amazed.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a clear 'k' at the end. The vowel is the same as 'cot' or 'caught' for most Americans, not the 'ah' of 'father' with a long sound; don't add a final 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'gawk' in informal speech to criticize someone staring at people, accidents or unusual things, for example 'Stop gawking at the tourists.' It can sound rude if used about a person in front of them, so use it with friends or about public scenes. The neutral alternative is 'stare' or 'look.'

distinctions.note: 'Stare' is neutral and can be a simple fixed look; 'gawk' implies an open, slack-jawed, somewhat foolish or rude stare.
'Gaze' is a calm, often admiring or thoughtful look; 'gawk' is clearly disapproving or mocking.
'Gape' focuses on the open mouth from surprise; 'gawk' focuses on the rude, staring behavior.

examples.everyday: Don't gawk at that man's tattoo; it's rude.
examples.professional: Please don't gawk at the new hire's laptop during the demo; just ask her about it.
examples.analytical: The crowd gawked at the wreckage, turning a private tragedy into a public spectacle.

nuance.analogy: Gawking is like leaving your mouth open at a magic show: you forget to look polite and just stare.
nuance.etymology: Probably from a Middle English or dialect word related to 'gaw' or 'gowk,' meaning cuckoo or fool.
common_mistakes: Using 'gawk' as a neutral synonym for 'look' in polite contexts; it sounds judgmental.
Saying 'gawk on' instead of 'gawk at.'

gawk.etymology: From a variant of *gowk*, from Middle English *gowke*, *goke*, from Old Norse *gaukr* (“cuckoo”), from Proto-Germanic **gaukaz* (“cuckoo”).

senses.definition: Of or relating to geometry.
senses.example: The architect used geometric techniques to design her home.

senses.definition: Increasing or decreasing in a geometric progression.
senses.example: Bacteria exhibit geometric increase in numbers when the environment is not limiting.

senses.definition: Using simple shapes such as circles, triangles, and lines in a decorative object.
senses.example: The building's profile was strikingly geometric.

core.definition: Of or relating to geometry, or built from simple shapes such as circles, triangles and straight lines.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, MET, and keep the last syllable as a quick reduced vowel, rik, not REEK. Americans say the r clearly, so do not drop it in the middle of the word.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use geometric in math classes, design, architecture and everyday talk about patterns, such as geometric tile or geometric earrings. In statistics and finance, geometric describes multiplicative growth, as in geometric mean or compound growth. In a meeting, saying growth is geometric usually means it is accelerating fast, which is an informal use.

distinctions.note: Arithmetic growth adds a fixed amount each step, while geometric growth multiplies by a fixed factor each step.
Geometrical is an older and less common form, and Americans usually prefer geometric in both technical and everyday use.

examples.everyday: The tiles in our new kitchen have a bold geometric pattern of triangles and circles.
examples.professional: Because usage doubles every quarter, the forecast is geometric, so we need to plan capacity for that curve.
examples.analytical: Euclid's geometric method builds all its theorems from a few definitions, postulates and common notions.

nuance.analogy: Geometric growth is like a snowball rolling downhill, gathering more snow with each turn.
nuance.etymology: From Greek geōmetrikos, from geōmetria, meaning land measurement.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the last syllable as REEK instead of a reduced rik.
Confusing geometric growth with fast growth in general; geometric means multiplicative, not just large.

geometric.etymology: From Latin *geōmetricus*, from Ancient Greek *γεωμετρικός*, from *γεωμέτρης*.

senses.definition: A member of the Hivite people of Gibeon, who tricked Joshua into a treaty and were later made servants of Israel.

core.definition: A member of the Hivite people of Gibeon, who tricked Joshua into a treaty and were later made servants of Israel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -ite is a long i sound, and the middle -ee- is a clear long e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to a people in Scripture and is used in Bible study and historical discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Gibeonite in Bible study, sermons and academic discussion of ancient Israel. It is not used in everyday talk. The term is usually a plural group reference, such as 'the Gibeonites'.

distinctions.note: Hivite is the broader ethnic group name in Scripture; Gibeonite refers specifically to the people of the city of Gibeon.

examples.everyday: At church, a woman asked about the Gibeonites, and I explained how they tricked Joshua with old sacks and bread.
examples.professional: In the sermon on covenant faithfulness, I used the Gibeonites to show that Israel's oath was binding even when it was won by deceit.
examples.analytical: The Gibeonites' status in Joshua 9 illustrates the tension between Israel's oath and its commandment to destroy the inhabitants of Canaan.

nuance.analogy: Like a group that wins a deal by a clever disguise and then must live under the terms, the Gibeonites embody a bargain that changed their whole future.
nuance.etymology: Derived from Gibeon, the name of the city.
common_mistakes: Using Gibeonite as a singular adjective without a noun, such as 'a Gibeonite man' when 'Gibeonite' is already a noun.
Confusing the Gibeonites with the Hivites in general.
nuance.biblical_note: The Gibeonites were a Hivite people (Joshua 9:7) who disguised themselves as travelers from a distant land and made a treaty with Israel (Joshua 9:3-15). Joshua honored the oath, and the Gibeonites became woodcutters and water carriers for the sanctuary (Joshua 9:27). In 2 Samuel 21:1-9, a famine is linked to Saul's violence against the Gibeonites, and the Gibeonites are given seven of Saul's descendants.

senses.definition: Showy but of poor quality; worthless.
Something showy but worthless; a bauble or gimmick.
To put together quickly and without much care; to bodge.
To embellish with gimcracks.

core.definition: Showy and attractive but cheaply made and of little value; worthless.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, JIM. Say the final syllable as a short, clipped krak, with no extra vowel after the k.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes things that look impressive but are shoddy, or ideas that dazzle without substance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gimcrack mostly in writing, reviews and formal criticism, and it sounds a little old-fashioned in casual speech. In everyday talk, people more often say cheap, flimsy, or junky. It can also be a noun meaning a showy, worthless trinket.

distinctions.note: Cheap can mean inexpensive, while gimcrack specifically implies showy decoration with poor quality.
Flimsy describes weak construction; gimcrack adds the sense of showy, shallow appeal.

examples.everyday: Don't buy that gimcrack lamp at the flea market, because it will fall apart in a week.
examples.professional: The vendor's dashboard looked impressive in the demo, but it was a gimcrack tool that broke on the first real query.
examples.analytical: A gimcrack argument may dazzle an audience, yet it lacks the structure to survive careful scrutiny.

nuance.analogy: A gimcrack item is like a shiny plastic toy on a store shelf: it catches the eye, then falls apart in your hands.
