nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; first recorded in the 1600s as a term for something showy and worthless.
common_mistakes: Using gimcrack for a neutral, well-made decorative object
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable

senses.definition: Of food, containing no gluten.
Of a person, not eating gluten.

core.definition: Containing no gluten, the protein found in wheat, barley and rye, so safe for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FREE, with a lighter secondary stress on GLOO. The middle syllable of gluten is a reduced schwa, so say GLOO-tuhn, not GLOO-ten.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it is a dietary label, and it can also be a health or lifestyle claim.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it constantly on restaurant menus, packaged food and in conversation about diets. Say 'Is this gluten-free?' when ordering, and expect staff to check ingredients if you have celiac disease. Only say you are gluten-free if you avoid it, since casual use for trendy diets is common and can be teased.

distinctions.note: Dairy-free means no milk products, which is a separate restriction; a dish can be gluten-free and still contain butter.
Celiac is a medical autoimmune condition, while gluten-free describes the food or the diet that treats it.

examples.everyday: Do you have any gluten-free desserts, or should I just skip dessert tonight?
examples.professional: Our catering vendor can supply gluten-free meals for the offsite, so please note dietary needs in the RSVP form.
examples.analytical: A gluten-free claim on a label is only meaningful when it is tied to a measurable threshold of gluten protein per serving.

nuance.analogy: Like a passport check at the border: the label certifies that something is missing what it might otherwise carry.
nuance.etymology: Gluten comes from Latin gluten, glue; free is from Old English freo, unrestricted.
common_mistakes: Saying GLOO-ten with a full vowel in the middle; the second syllable is reduced.
Using gluten-free for food that is simply low in carbs; it refers only to gluten.

conversation.text: Do you have any gluten-free pasta or bread?
My sister is gluten-free, so we need a place with options.
The pizza crust can be made gluten-free for two dollars extra.

senses.definition: A giant; a much bigger, stronger opponent, as in "a David-and-Goliath fight".
The giant Philistine warrior from Gath whom the young David defeated with a sling and stone.

core.definition: The giant Philistine warrior from Gath whom the young David defeated with a sling and stone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, which has the long i sound. The first syllable is a reduced schwa, and the final th is voiceless as in think.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the Bible, and used in everyday English to describe a much stronger opponent or a huge thing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Goliath in everyday speech for a much larger or more powerful opponent, usually in the phrase David and Goliath, which describes an underdog victory. The name is also used for huge objects or companies. It is informal but widely understood.
word_family: Goliath (noun, as a common noun for a giant)

distinctions.note: Giant is a general word for a very large being or thing; Goliath names the specific Bible figure and is often used as a metaphor for a formidable opponent.
David is the young underdog who wins; Goliath is the strong opponent he defeats.

examples.everyday: Our small bakery is fighting a Goliath of a chain store, but people love our bread.
examples.professional: Our startup is competing with a Goliath in the cloud market, so we need a sharper strategy.
examples.analytical: The story of David and Goliath has been read as a model of faith confronting overwhelming power.

nuance.analogy: Goliath is like the heavyweight champion in a boxing match who looks unbeatable until someone uses a surprising tool to win.
nuance.etymology: The name is of uncertain origin and is often linked to a possible Philistine or Anatolian source; the etymology is not firmly established.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as GOL-ee-ath; the stress is on the second syllable.
Pronouncing the final th as a t or d.
nuance.biblical_note: Goliath is the Philistine champion of Gath who challenges Israel's army in 1 Samuel 17. 1 Samuel 17:4 describes him as a warrior of great height, about six cubits and a span. In 1 Samuel 17:49 David strikes him with a stone from a sling, and in 17:50 David kills him and takes his sword. The story shows God's power working through a young shepherd rather than through armor or size.

senses.definition: A fine film made up of cobwebs, seen floating in the air or caught on bushes, etc.
A soft, sheer fabric.
Anything delicate, light and flimsy.
Tenuous, light, filmy or delicate.

core.definition: A very fine, light, filmy substance, such as spider silk or thin, sheer fabric.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Many learners add an extra syllable as in 'GAH-suh-mare', but the final syllable is the reduced American 'er' sound.

nuance.connotation: positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'gossamer' mainly in literary writing, poetry, or descriptions of delicate things, such as a morning web or a fabric. In everyday speech, people usually say 'spider web' or 'sheer fabric' instead. The word is often used figuratively, as in 'gossamer dreams'.

distinctions.note: Silk is a material from silkworms, while gossamer describes something so thin and light that it seems almost weightless.
Sheer is a common everyday term for thin see-through fabric, while gossamer is more poetic and emphasizes delicacy.

examples.everyday: Look at that gossamer web on the bush, it's covered in dew this morning.
examples.professional: The designer chose a gossamer chiffon for the summer collection because it drapes so lightly.
examples.analytical: The poet's gossamer imagery suggests that the speaker's memories are fragile and easily lost.

nuance.analogy: Gossamer is like a breath made visible: you can see it, but it hardly seems to have any weight.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; possibly from Middle English gosesomer, perhaps from 'goose summer', the season when such threads drift in the air.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'gos-a-mer' with the stress on the wrong syllable.
Using 'gossamer' for thick or heavy things, when the word always implies lightness.

senses.definition: The state of being grateful.
senses.example: She showed deep gratitude for the support she received.

core.definition: The feeling of being thankful and appreciative for something received.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllables are weak, and the final syllable is 'tood', not 'tyood'. The 't' in the middle often sounds like a soft flap in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It expresses warmth and appreciation, and is used sincerely in personal and public settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'gratitude' in heartfelt or reflective contexts, such as thanking someone at a dinner, in a toast, or in a formal letter. In everyday thank-yous, 'thanks' or 'thank you so much' is more typical. 'Gratitude' often appears in phrases like 'with gratitude' or 'express gratitude.'

distinctions.note: 'Thanks' is the everyday, casual word. 'Gratitude' is deeper and more formal, often used in writing or speeches.
'Appreciation' can mean recognizing value or quality in something. 'Gratitude' specifically means thankfulness for a benefit received.

examples.everyday: I just want you to know how much gratitude I feel for everything you did while I was sick.
examples.professional: On behalf of the team, I want to express our gratitude for your support during the launch.
examples.analytical: Gratitude, in many moral accounts, is the emotion that acknowledges a gift as unearned and binds giver and receiver together.

nuance.analogy: Like a warm coat on a cold day, gratitude wraps you in the feeling that someone helped you.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin 'gratitudo', from Latin 'gratus' (pleasing, thankful).
common_mistakes: Using 'gratitude' as a verb, as in 'I gratitude you'.
Saying 'gratitudes' in the plural when meaning thanks in general.

senses.definition: Freely; in the manner of a gift, without being earned.
In a manner not demanded by the circumstances, without reason, justification, cause, or proof.

core.definition: In a way that is unnecessary or unjustified, without reason or need.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the 'TOO' syllable. Keep the endings weak: the '-ously' ends as 'us-lee'. Do not pronounce the 'ou' as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes actions or remarks that are uncalled for and often hurtful or offensive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'gratuitously' in news reporting, reviews, and criticism to describe violence, insults, or details that seem to serve no purpose. In casual speech, people more often say 'for no reason' or 'just to be mean'. The word sounds more formal than the everyday phrases.

distinctions.note: 'Needlessly' is the everyday word for doing something that did not have to be done. 'Gratuitously' adds a stronger sense of deliberate excess.
'Unnecessarily' is neutral and common. 'Gratuitously' is more formal and suggests the act was hurtful or excessive.

examples.everyday: He didn't have to say that, but he gratuitously brought up my old mistake in front of everybody.
examples.professional: The report gratuitously repeated the same chart three times, which made the document longer without adding insight.
examples.analytical: The film depicts violence gratuitously, so critics argue the scenes exist more for shock value than for narrative purpose.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who speeds through a school zone for no reason, the action is excessive and unjustified.
nuance.etymology: From 'gratuitous' plus '-ly', from Latin 'gratuitus' (given freely).
common_mistakes: Using it as a positive word meaning 'generously'.
Mispronouncing the stress as 'GRAT-u-ous-ly'.

senses.definition: To reduce to smaller pieces by crushing with lateral motion.
To shape with the force of friction.
senses.example: grind a lens; grind an axe

senses.definition: To remove material by rubbing with an abrasive surface.
To become ground, pulverized, or polished by friction.
senses.example: This corn grinds well.

senses.definition: To move with much difficulty or friction; to grate.
To oppress, hold down or weaken.
To rotate the hips erotically.
To dance in a sexually suggestive way with both partners in very close proximity, often pressed against each other.
To rub one's body against another's in a sexual way; to frottage.
To repeat a task a large number of times in a row to achieve a specific goal.
senses.example: These enemies give lots of loot when killed, so many players fight them to grind for resources.

senses.definition: To operate by turning a crank.
senses.example: to grind an organ

senses.definition: To produce mechanically and repetitively as if by turning a crank.
To eat.
senses.example: Eh, brah, let's go grind.

senses.definition: To instill through repetitive teaching.
senses.example: Grinding lessons into students' heads does not motivate them to learn.

senses.definition: To work or study hard; to hustle or drudge.
senses.example: to grind LeetCode

senses.definition: To annoy or irritate (a person); to grind one's gears.
To slide the flat portion of a skateboard or snowboard across an obstacle such as a railing.
To automatically format and indent code.
The act of reducing to powder, or of sharpening, by friction.
Something that has been reduced to powder, something that has been ground.
A specific degree of pulverization of coffee beans.
senses.example: This bag contains espresso grind.

senses.definition: A tedious and laborious task.
senses.example: This homework is a grind.

senses.definition: A grinding trick on a skateboard or snowboard.
Clipping of grindcore (“subgenre of heavy metal”).
Hustle; hard work.
senses.example: I've been on the grind all week, trying to make ends meet.

senses.definition: A traditional communal pilot whale hunt in the Faroe Islands.

core.definition: To crush something into small pieces or powder by pressing and rubbing it between hard surfaces.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is a long "eye" diphthong, and the d at the end is clearly pronounced. Do not add a vowel after the d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses; it can be negative when it describes hard, tedious work ("the daily grind").
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "grind" for coffee beans, pepper, meat and in phrases about tedious work. The noun "the daily grind" is a common, casual way to describe routine work. Saying someone is "grinding" can also mean studying or working very hard.

distinctions.note: "Crush" means breaking something by pressure; "grind" specifically implies rubbing or friction to make powder or fine pieces.
"Mill" is a machine or building for grinding grain; "grind" is the action.

examples.everyday: Could you grind some pepper over my pasta, please?
examples.professional: We need to grind the raw data into smaller batches before the model can process it.
examples.analytical: The author argues that bureaucratic routine can grind down the moral imagination of ordinary workers.

nuance.analogy: Like a millstone turning slowly over wheat: steady pressure gradually turns something solid into fine dust.
nuance.etymology: From Old English grindan, to crush or rub.
common_mistakes: Confusing "grind" (to crush) with "grand" in speech.
Using "grind" for simply cutting or chopping food.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, grinding is a common image of daily labor and humiliation, especially at the mill. The Hebrew word tahan means to grind, and the Greek word aleuo means to grind at a mill. Judges 16:21 describes Samson forced to grind grain in prison after his capture. Matthew 24:41 describes two women grinding at the mill, one taken and one left, as a sign of sudden judgment. Ecclesiastes 12:3 uses the image of grinders ceasing as a poetic picture of old age.

grind.etymology: From Middle English *grynden*, from Old English *grindan* (“to grind”), from **grindan*, from Proto-Germanic **grindaną* (“to crush, grind”).

senses.definition: To lift with difficulty; to raise with some effort; to lift (a heavy thing).
senses.example: We heaved the chest-of-drawers up to the second-floor landing.

senses.definition: To throw, cast.
senses.example: They hove rocks into the pond.

senses.definition: To rise and fall.
senses.example: Her chest heaved with emotion.

senses.definition: To utter with effort.
senses.example: She heaved a sigh and stared out of the window.

senses.definition: To be thrown up or raised; to rise upward, as a tower or mound.
To retch, to make an effort to vomit; to vomit.
senses.example: The smell of the old cheese was enough to make you heave.

senses.definition: To make an effort to raise, throw, or move anything; to strain to do something difficult.
To pull up with a rope or cable.
senses.example: Heave up the anchor there, boys!

senses.definition: To displace (a vein, stratum).
To move in a certain direction or into a certain position or situation.
senses.example: to heave the ship ahead

senses.definition: An effort to raise something, such as a weight or one's own body, or to move something heavy.
senses.example: We gave one more heave and the wall toppled over at last.

senses.definition: An upward motion; a rising; a swell or distention, as of the breast in difficult breathing, of the waves, of the earth in an earthquake, etc.
A horizontal dislocation in a metallic lode, taking place at an intersection with another lode.
An effort to vomit; retching.
The measure of extent to which a nautical vessel goes up and down in a short period of time.
A forceful shot in which the ball follows a high trajectory.
Broken wind in horses.

core.definition: To lift or pull something heavy with great effort, often by pushing or straining.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single syllable with a long 'ee' vowel and a voiced final 'v'. Don't devoice the final sound to 'f', and don't confuse it with 'have' or 'heavy'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly informal. It describes physical effort and can sound vivid in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use heave most often in casual speech about lifting heavy objects, such as 'heave the couch up the stairs'. In the phrase 'heave a sigh' it is more literary. Many Americans also say 'lift' or 'haul' in neutral contexts, so heave can sound a little dramatic.

distinctions.note: Lift is the neutral, general word for raising something, while heave suggests more effort and a heavier load.
Haul often means pulling or carrying something over a distance, while heave focuses on the upward push or throw.

examples.everyday: Can you help me heave this couch into the back of the truck?
examples.professional: The movers had to heave the server rack onto the loading dock, so we need a lift gate next time.
examples.analytical: In the narrative, the speaker's heave of breath signals not only exertion but the weight of the moment.

nuance.analogy: Heave is like a tug-of-war rope pulled hard and lifted, requiring your whole body rather than just your hands.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hebban 'to lift', related to the root of heavy.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing it as 'have' with a short vowel; the vowel is long 'ee'.
Using heave for light lifting, where lift is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible, the term 'heave offering' in the RSV translates Hebrew terumah, meaning a contribution or portion set apart for the priests. Exodus 29:27 describes the breast and thigh portions of the ram of ordination as heave offerings belonging to Aaron and his sons. Numbers 15:19-20 instructs Israel to present a heave offering from the first of their bread dough to the Lord.

heave.etymology: From Middle English *heven*, *hebben*, from Old English *hebban*, from **habbjan*, from Proto-Germanic **habjaną* (“to take up, lift”), from Proto-Indo-European **kapyéti*, from the root **kap-*.

senses.definition: The abode of God or the gods, traditionally conceived as beyond the sky; especially:
The abode of God and of the angels and saints in His presence.
The abode of the Abrahamic God; similar abodes of the gods in other religions and traditions, such as Mount Olympus.
The afterlife of the blessed dead, traditionally conceived as opposed to an afterlife of the wicked and unjust (compare hell).
Paradise, the afterlife of the souls who are not sent to a place of punishment or purification such as hell, purgatory, or limbo; the state or condition of being in the presence of God after death.
The afterlife of the blessed dead in other religions and traditions, such as the Pure Land or Elysium.
The sky.
Providence, the will of God or the council of the gods; fate.
Any paradise; any blissful place or experience.
A state of bliss; a peaceful ecstasy.
Similarly blissful afterlives, places, or states for particular people, animals, or objects.
The distant sky in which the sun, moon, and stars appear or move; the firmament; the celestial spheres.

core.definition: The place where God and the angels live, traditionally thought of as above the sky; the afterlife for the faithful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is reduced to a schwa-like 'un', so don't add a full 'ahn'. The 'v' is voiced, not like an 'f'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests peace, reward, and joy, and it is used both in religious and everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use heaven in religious conversation, in funerals, and in everyday expressions like 'thank heaven' or 'heaven knows'. Saying 'Oh my heavens' is informal and sometimes sounds old-fashioned. In a religious setting, use it with respect; in casual speech, it often sounds emotional rather than doctrinal.

distinctions.note: Sky is the physical atmosphere above us, while heaven is a spiritual or religious place of God.
Paradise often means an ideal, peaceful place on earth or in the afterlife, while heaven is specifically the abode of God and the faithful.

examples.everyday: After the funeral, my neighbor said she hoped her husband was in heaven now.
examples.professional: In the team retrospective, someone joked that the new deployment pipeline was a little bit of heaven.
examples.analytical: The doctrine of heaven shapes a theology of hope, since it names the final communion of creatures with God.

nuance.analogy: Heaven is like the home you return to after a long journey, a place of rest and belonging.
nuance.etymology: From Old English heofon, 'sky' or 'heaven', from Germanic roots meaning 'raised' or 'covering'.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable such as 'HEV-en-uh' rather than a reduced final 'un'.
Using heaven in a purely physical sense to mean sky in ordinary speech, which can sound oddly poetic.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible, heaven translates shamayim, referring to the sky and to God's dwelling above it. In the Greek New Testament it translates ouranos, which can mean sky or the dwelling place of God. Genesis 1:1 names God as creator of the heavens and the earth. Matthew 6:9 begins the Lord's Prayer by addressing the Father 'who art in heaven', which places God's rule above the world.

heaven.etymology: From a wide variety of Middle English forms including *hevene*, *heven*, *hevin* and *hewin* (“heaven, sky”), from Old English *heofon*, *heofone* (“heaven, sky”), from **hebun* (“heaven, sky”), of uncertain origin.

senses.definition: The qualities characteristic of a hero, such as courage, bravery, fortitude, selflessness, etc. the display of such qualities.

core.definition: Great courage and selflessness shown in dangerous situations, or the qualities that make someone a hero.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HEH. The final -ism is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'iz-um,' not 'iz-em.'

nuance.connotation: Positive; it expresses admiration for courage and self-sacrifice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use heroism for moral courage in emergencies, military service and everyday acts of sacrifice. It is common in news stories and speeches, such as honoring firefighters or veterans. In casual talk, people often say 'that was so brave' instead.

distinctions.note: Courage is the general quality of facing fear; heroism is courage shown in extraordinary service, often to others.
Bravery is more casual and personal; heroism is more formal and suggests public or moral significance.

examples.everyday: The way she pulled her neighbor out of the car was pure heroism.
examples.professional: The company honored the employee whose quick action showed real heroism during the evacuation.
examples.analytical: For Aristotle, heroism is not mere daring but the excellence of character that makes a person act nobly under pressure.

nuance.analogy: Heroism is like a candle in a dark room, showing light when most people would stay in the shadows.
nuance.etymology: From hero plus the suffix -ism, from Greek hērōs, 'hero.'
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the last syllable as 'izm' with a clear vowel.
Using heroism for a single small kindness; it usually implies greater risk or sacrifice.

senses.definition: Leave out an ingredient: "a burger, hold the onions" means no onions.

core.definition: Ask for something to be left out of a food or drink order, such as a sauce or ingredient.

pronunciation.tip: In this phrase hold is stressed and the is reduced to a short uh sound, so say HOHLD thuh, not HOHLD thee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite. It is a normal request in restaurants, but it can sound abrupt without a please.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in fast food, sandwich shops and casual restaurants, often with an ingredient after it, as in 'a burger, hold the onions.' It is informal and very common. A natural reply is 'Sure, no onions' or 'Got it.' At a sit-down restaurant, you may also say 'without onions' or 'no onions, please.'

distinctions.note: No is simpler and common, while hold the is the typical phrase in counter service and fast food.
Without is more formal and polished, while hold the is casual and very common in fast food ordering.

examples.everyday: I'll have a cheeseburger, hold the pickles, please.
examples.professional: For the team lunch, can you get the sandwiches with hold the mayo for two people?
examples.analytical: The phrase hold the reveals how ordering language is built around omission rather than full description.

nuance.analogy: Like crossing a name off a guest list, hold the removes one item from the order.
common_mistakes: Using hold the as a complete phrase without naming the ingredient.
Saying hold the onion with singular countability in ordering, when Americans usually say hold the onions.

conversation.text: I'll have a cheeseburger, but hold the onions, please.
Can I get a turkey sandwich? Hold the mayo.
Can I get the tacos? Hold the cilantro, please.

senses.definition: To join a phone call or video call.
To begin playing a video game.
To reprimand or scold (someone); to attack or beat up (someone).
To begin a course of PEDs (performance-enhancing drugs, e.g. steroids).
senses.example: I don't think you should hop on like those guys because it's harmful to your health.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see hop,‎ on.

core.definition: To join a phone or video call, or to get on a bus, train, or other vehicle quickly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ON, and in American speech on is pronounced with the same vowel as in lot. Link the two words, so it sounds like hah-PAHN.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans say hop on a call or hop on a Zoom in relaxed workplace talk. It is informal, so use join in formal writing. Hop on a bus or train is common in city life, meaning to board quickly. The aggressive senses listed in dictionaries are rare in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Join is the neutral and formal word for entering a call or meeting, while hop on is informal and suggests doing it quickly.
Get on is the standard term for boarding a vehicle, and hop on adds a sense of speed and ease.

examples.everyday: Hop on the bus with me, it's faster than walking.
examples.professional: Can you hop on the call at three? We need your input on the budget.
examples.analytical: Early adopters hop on new platforms quickly, but their enthusiasm often obscures the costs of migration.

nuance.analogy: Like jumping onto a moving bus with one quick motion.
nuance.etymology: From hop (Old English hoppian, to leap) and on.
common_mistakes: Saying hop on the call instead of hop on a call, which omits the article in a common pattern.
Confusing hop on with hop off, which means the opposite.

conversation.text: Hop on the next train; it's right behind this one.
Hop on; I'll give you a ride.
Can you hop on a quick call at two?

senses.definition: Abbreviation of high-occupancy vehicle lane.

core.definition: A traffic lane on a highway reserved for vehicles carrying two or more people, or certain low-emission vehicles.

pronunciation.tip: Americans say the letters H, O and V one at a time, with the main stress on the letter V (vee). Do not say the abbreviation as a single word like 'hov'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical traffic term that drivers use constantly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in everyday driving conversation, as in 'Let's take the HOV lane so we get there faster.' Drivers alone in a car may use the lane only if the vehicle is a qualifying low-emission type, and enforcement varies by state. Some lanes use a diamond symbol on the road, and the rules are posted on signs.

distinctions.note: Carpool lane is a common informal name, while HOV lane is the official and more widely used term on signs and in news.
An express lane may be for any vehicle that pays a toll or has low traffic, while an HOV lane is restricted by the number of people in the car.

examples.everyday: Hop in the HOV lane with me, since we have two people in the car and the traffic's terrible.
examples.professional: Our commute policy allows carpool drivers to use the HOV lane when the team travels together to the client site.
examples.analytical: HOV lanes are an example of congestion policy that trades a public road's capacity for an incentive to share rides, which raises questions about equity and efficiency.

nuance.analogy: Like a priority boarding line for groups traveling together, it rewards sharing a ride.
nuance.etymology: HOV is an abbreviation of 'high-occupancy vehicle', a term from U.S. transportation planning in the 1970s.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'HOV' as one word, like 'hov' or 'hove', instead of saying the letters H-O-V.
Assuming the HOV lane is open to any car; the passenger count or vehicle type matters.

conversation.text: The HOV lane is only for cars with two or more people during rush hour.
In some cities, the HOV lane opens to everyone after 7 p.m.
Take the HOV lane; there are three of us in the car.

senses.definition: Behavior exhibiting excessive or uncontrollable emotions, in a wide range from joy to panic but usually including anxiety or fear.
Synonym of conversion disorder.
Any disorder of women with some psychiatric symptoms without other diagnosis, ascribed to uterine influences on the female body, lack of pregnancy, or lack of sex.
A mental disorder characterized by emotional excitability etc. without an organic cause.

core.definition: Extreme, uncontrollable emotion, such as panic or fear, that spreads through a crowd or erupts suddenly in one person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, STEH, not on the first. The final -ia is a light, reduced vowel, not a separate 'ya' sound, and the r is clearly pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Negative. The word describes a loss of control and is often used to suggest that a reaction is excessive or irrational.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hysteria for intense panic or wild emotion, especially in a group, such as mass hysteria during a crisis or news frenzy. Calling a person hysterical is an insult that implies they are overreacting, so use it carefully. The old medical sense of a women's disorder is outdated and should not be used today.

distinctions.note: Panic is a sudden fear that drives you to flee, while hysteria is broader and often involves crying, screaming or laughter that you cannot control.
Hysterics in the plural is informal and can mean uncontrolled laughing or crying, while hysteria is the more formal, general noun.

examples.everyday: The whole street fell into hysteria when the power went out at midnight.
examples.professional: The social media coverage of the outage created mass hysteria, so we need a calm, factual update for our customers.
examples.analytical: Scholars of crowd behavior argue that collective hysteria spreads fastest when people cannot verify what they are told.

nuance.analogy: Like a fire that jumps from one dry leaf to the next, hysteria spreads from person to person faster than the facts can catch up.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hystera, meaning womb, from an old belief that the disorder came from the uterus.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as HIS-teria; the stress belongs on -STEH-.
Calling a coworker hysterical in a disagreement, which sounds dismissive and can be offensive; choose calm or upset instead.

hysteria.etymology: From New Latin *hysteria*, a back-formation from Latin *hystericus*, from Ancient Greek *ὑστερικός* (“suffering in the uterus, hysterical”), from *ὑστέρα* (“womb”).

senses.definition: Consisting of iambs (metrical feet with an unstressed–stressed pattern) or characterized by their predominance.
An iamb; a line or group of lines of iambs.

core.definition: Describing verse built on iambs, the pattern of one unstressed syllable followed by one stressed syllable.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on AM, the middle syllable. The b is pronounced, and the final -ic is short, like 'pick,' not 'bike.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term in literary analysis.
nuance.usage_note: English teachers, poets and literary critics use this adjective to describe rhythm, as in 'iambic pentameter.' Ordinary Americans rarely use it outside school or poetry discussions. The noun use, an iambic, exists but is rare.

distinctions.note: Trochaic describes verse with a stressed then unstressed pattern, the reverse of iambic.
Dactylic describes verse with one stressed syllable followed by two unstressed syllables.

examples.everyday: Shakespeare usually writes in iambic lines, which is why they sound so steady.
examples.professional: The rhythm of the poem is iambic, so the reading group can mark the stresses easily.
examples.analytical: The poem maintains an iambic pattern throughout, though the poet varies the expected stress at key moments.

nuance.analogy: Like a steady two-beat walking rhythm: step-STEP, step-STEP.
nuance.etymology: From iamb, from Greek iambos, a verse form.
common_mistakes: Saying 'eye-AM-bic' with a hard c sound instead of a k sound.
Using iambic to describe prose or everyday speech; it applies only to metrical verse.

iambic.etymology: From Middle French *iambique*, from Late Latin *ïambicus*, from Ancient Greek *ἰαμβικός*, from *ἴαμβος* + *-ικός*.

senses.definition: A number of the form bi, where b is any real number and i denotes the imaginary unit.
A number of the form a + bi, where a and b are real numbers and b is nonzero.

core.definition: A number of the form bi, where b is a real number and i is the imaginary unit, the square root of minus one.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MAJ in imaginary and NUM in number. In American speech, number is said NUM-ber with a reduced final syllable, so do not add an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise mathematical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use imaginary number in math classes and technical discussions about complex numbers. The name is historical and does not mean the number is unreal. In a class or meeting, say 'the imaginary part of a complex number' when you need precision, and remember that imaginary numbers are fully valid in mathematics.

distinctions.note: A complex number is a number a + bi with real parts a and b; an imaginary number is the special case where a is zero.
A real number lies on the number line; an imaginary number is not on that line, though both are used in complex analysis.

collocations: the square root of a negative number

examples.everyday: My son's homework asked about imaginary numbers, and I had to remember that they are not actually imaginary at all.
examples.professional: The signal processing code stores the imaginary part separately, since the Fourier transform produces complex outputs.
examples.analytical: The historical name imaginary number reflects early resistance to these quantities, yet they became essential to algebra and physics.

nuance.analogy: An imaginary number is like a second compass direction: it points off the number line, giving you a new dimension rather than a fake one.
nuance.etymology: The term was coined by René Descartes in the 17th century as a somewhat dismissive label.
common_mistakes: Thinking imaginary numbers are not real or useful; they are essential in engineering and physics.
Stressing the words evenly; the main stress falls on MAJ in imaginary and NUM in number.

imaginary-number.etymology: The adjective imaginary in this context was first used (as French *imaginaire*) by René Descartes in 1673, La Geometrie, referring to imaginary numbers in the broad sense, as non-real roots of polynomials.

senses.definition: Perfect, without faults, flaws or errors.
senses.example: He grew up in Norway, but he writes impeccable English.

senses.definition: Incapable of wrongdoing or sin; immaculate.
senses.example: It was easy for James V to imprison Lady Glamis, but actually convicting her was far more difficult; her character was impeccable and she was highly respected by all who knew her.

core.definition: Perfect, with no flaws or mistakes; so well done that nothing could be improved.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, PEK. The middle vowel is short and reduced, so say 'PEK-uh-buhl', not 'im-PEEK-uh-buhl'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises high standards, but can sound slightly stiff when used for ordinary things.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use impeccable for appearance, manners, service or work quality, such as 'impeccable taste' or 'impeccable manners'. In casual talk people more often say perfect or flawless. It is a good word for a compliment about a restaurant, a presentation or a colleague's report.

distinctions.note: Perfect is the everyday, general word and can describe anything with no defects. Impeccable adds a sense of high standards and is often used about manners, dress or conduct.
Flawless focuses on the absence of visible defects, often in physical objects or performances. Impeccable has a broader sense that includes behavior and taste.

examples.everyday: The waiter at that new place was impeccable, refilling our water before we even asked.
examples.professional: Her slide deck was impeccable, with every chart labeled and every number checked twice before the client meeting.
examples.analytical: Kant's ideal of moral action is impeccable in its logic, yet critics ask whether any human agent can meet it.

nuance.analogy: Like a freshly ironed shirt with not one wrinkle, impeccable means nothing is out of place.
nuance.etymology: From Latin in- (not) plus peccare (to sin, err), so literally 'not able to sin' and later 'without fault'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'peek' instead of a short 'puh'.
Using impeccable for ordinary, unremarkable things; it is a strong word of praise.

impeccable.etymology: From Middle French *impeccable*, from Latin *impeccabilis* (“not liable to sin”), from *im-* (“not”) + *pecco* (“to err, to sin”).

senses.definition: The property of being inaccurate; lack of accuracy.
A statement, passage etc. that is inaccurate or false.
Incorrect calibration of a measuring device, or incorrect use; lack of precision.
A move that is considered suboptimal, but not as bad as a mistake or blunder.

core.definition: A mistake or error in information, a measurement, or a statement; a fact or detail that is not correct.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, AK. Say the middle syllables quickly and lightly, and keep the American r-colored vowel in the -yer- part, not a hard 'you-ray'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names a flaw or error, and it is often used to correct someone politely or to point out problems in data or reporting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use inaccuracy in both casual and professional speech, for example 'There are some inaccuracies in the report.' It sounds more measured than 'mistake' and is common in journalism, science and business. To say something is wrong with less formality, Americans often say 'That's not right' or 'You got that wrong.'

distinctions.note: An error is any mistake, often a slip in process or judgment, while inaccuracy describes a lack of correspondence to the truth or to a standard, often in facts or measurements.
Imprecision means vagueness or lack of exactness in detail, while inaccuracy means the result is actually wrong, even if it looks exact.

examples.everyday: My uncle pointed out a few inaccuracies in the story the local paper ran about his farm.
examples.professional: The QA team flagged several inaccuracies in the dashboard before we sent it to the client.
examples.analytical: The argument rests on a historical inaccuracy that undermines its central claim about the council's origins.

nuance.analogy: Like a map with a few streets in the wrong place: most of it helps, but the errors can send you the wrong way.
nuance.etymology: From in- (not) plus accuracy, from Latin accuratus, 'done with care'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable (in-AK-yer-uh-see, not IN-ak-yer-uh-see).
Using inaccuracy for a person's character flaw; use 'inaccuracy' only for facts, data or statements.

senses.definition: An incarnate being or form.
A version or iteration (of something).
A living being embodying a deity or spirit.
An assumption of human form or nature.
A person or thing regarded as embodying or exhibiting some quality, idea, or the like.
senses.example: The leading dancer is the incarnation of grace.

senses.definition: The act of incarnating.
The state of being incarnated.
A rosy or red color; flesh (the color); carnation.

core.definition: The doctrine that God the Son took on human flesh in Jesus Christ. Also a living embodiment of a quality or a particular version of something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -NAY-. The first syllable is /ɪn/, not /ɪŋ/, and the ending is 'shun', not 'tee-on'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in religious and academic contexts; figuratively it can be positive, as 'the incarnation of good taste', or neutral, as 'the latest incarnation'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in churches, seminaries and religious studies, and in a general sense for a new version of something ('the third incarnation of the software'). In casual talk you might hear 'version' or 'form' instead. In a church discussion, 'the Incarnation' with a capital I refers to Christmas theology.

distinctions.note: Embodiment is the general word for a person or thing that expresses a quality; incarnation adds the sense of a being taking bodily form.
Version is a neutral, everyday word for a new form of a product or idea; incarnation is more formal and suggests a fuller, more embodied form.

examples.everyday: This year's blender is the fourth incarnation of the same design, and honestly it's the best one yet.
examples.professional: The new dashboard is the latest incarnation of our reporting pipeline, so please update your bookmarks.
examples.analytical: The doctrine of the Incarnation holds that the eternal Son took on human nature without ceasing to be fully divine.

nuance.analogy: Like a song that is recorded again and again: each recording is a new form of the same melody, but the Incarnation is the melody taking on a voice.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin incarnatio, from incarnare 'to make flesh', from in- and caro, carnis 'flesh'.
common_mistakes: Saying /ɪŋ/ for the first syllable; the n should be pronounced as in 'in'.
Using 'incarnation' as a verb; the verb is 'incarnate'.
Writing 'incarnation' in lowercase when referring to the doctrine of Christ; the capital I marks the theological sense.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind the idea is sarx, 'flesh'. John 1:14 states that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Colossians 2:9 says that in Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily. 1 John 4:2 affirms that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

incarnation.etymology: From Middle English *incarnacion*, borrowed from Old French *incarnacion*, from Medieval Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin *incarnatio*, from Late Latin *incarnari* (“to be made flesh”).

senses.definition: That which cannot be precisely defined or put into words.
That which defies description; indescribable.
Anything that cannot be defined.

core.definition: Too vague, subtle, or complex to be precisely defined or described in words.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'FY', the third syllable, as in 'define'. The final -able is a reduced 'uh-bul', not 'ay-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests a special quality that resists description.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in writing, reviews, and conversation about a feeling, a flavor, or an atmosphere that is hard to name. In casual speech people often say 'I can't put my finger on it'. It can sound a little dramatic if overused.

distinctions.note: Indescribable stresses that words fail to capture something; indefinable stresses that its boundaries or nature cannot be fixed.
Vague is a general negative term about unclearness; indefinable is more neutral and often used for subtle qualities.

examples.everyday: This little café has an indefinable charm that makes you want to stay all afternoon.
examples.professional: The product has an indefinable quality that customers love, but it is hard to write into the spec.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's concept of virtue remains indefinable in purely quantitative terms, which is part of its appeal.

nuance.analogy: Like a smell in a room: you notice it clearly, but you cannot name its exact ingredients.
nuance.etymology: From in- 'not' + definable, from Latin definire 'to define'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'undefinable' in formal writing; both are used, but 'indefinable' is more common.
Putting stress on 'in' rather than 'FY'.

senses.definition: The principle that if two objects are absolutely identical then they must be indistinguishable from one another with respect to all of their properties.

core.definition: The philosophical principle that if two things are truly identical, they cannot differ in any property, so no property can tell them apart.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BIL in indiscernibility and on DEN in identicals. Say 'of' as a weak 'uv', and link the words smoothly in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: neutral; a precise technical term used in logic and metaphysics with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Philosophers and logicians use this phrase, usually in its shorter form 'Leibniz's Law', when arguing about identity and properties. Americans in conversation rarely say it, so in ordinary talk you would say 'if two things are exactly the same, they have all the same properties'. It is often paired with the converse, the identity of indiscernibles.

distinctions.note: The converse principle: things with all the same properties must be identical. Leibniz held both principles, but they are logically distinct claims.
Another name for the same principle, used more often in American philosophy classrooms.

examples.everyday: I can't explain it well, but my professor says the indiscernibility of identicals means two identical things can't differ in any way.
examples.professional: In the model specification review, we used the indiscernibility of identicals to argue that the two feature sets were redundant.
examples.analytical: The argument from the indiscernibility of identicals presupposes that every property is an intrinsic or relational feature that can be included in a complete description of an object.

nuance.analogy: Like two copies of a key cut from exactly the same mold: if they match in every measurement, there is no way to tell which one is which.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'indiscernibilis' (not distinguishable), from 'in-' (not) plus 'discernere' (to separate, distinguish) and 'identicus' (the same).
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'in-dis-ser-NIB-il-ity' instead of 'in-dih-sur-nuh-BIL-ih-tee'.
Confusing the principle with the converse, which is the identity of indiscernibles.

senses.definition: The tendency for a person to act without reference to others, particularly in matters of style, fashion or mode of thought.

The moral stance, political philosophy, or social outlook that promotes independence and self-reliance of individual people, while opposing the interference with each person's choices by society, the state, or any other group or institution.
The doctrine that only individual things are real.
The doctrine that nothing exists but the individual self.

core.definition: The belief that people should act independently and make their own choices, valuing personal freedom over group or state control.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on VIH, the third syllable. Keep the middle syllables quick and reduced, and the final '-ism' is a short 'izm' with a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Often positive, linked to freedom and self-reliance; can be negative when it suggests selfishness or disregard for others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often discuss individualism as a core national value, linked to independence, the frontier and the self-made person. In casual talk, calling someone an individualist can be a compliment or a criticism, depending on tone. In politics and academic debate, it is central, often contrasted with collectivism or community.

distinctions.note: Individualism is a belief or philosophy; individuality is the quality of being distinct from others.
Selfishness is a negative focus on oneself; individualism is a principled stance that emphasizes personal choice and independence.

examples.everyday: My brother is all about individualism; he refuses to follow any trend.
examples.professional: Our team culture values individualism in problem solving, but we still expect everyone to share their code.
examples.analytical: Tocqueville saw American individualism as a double-edged virtue, fostering independence while weakening civic bonds.

nuance.analogy: Like a lone tree on a hill that grows its own shape, unlike trees planted in a row.
nuance.etymology: Formed from individual plus the suffix -ism; the word appeared in the 19th century.
common_mistakes: Using it to mean 'individuality' (the quality of being unique), when it refers to a belief or social outlook.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in in-dih-vih-DJOO-uh-lizm.

senses.definition: A similar period of play.
senses.example: We batted around in our half of the inning.

senses.definition: A player (or team)'s turn at the table to make shots until ended by a miss or a foul.
A chance or opportunity to perform some deed or act.
senses.example: We are in just the second inning of our quest to enter this new market.

senses.definition: A period of play in which members of a visiting baseball team attempt to hit a baseball pitched by the opposing home team until three players are called out, followed by a similar attempt by members of the home baseball team against the visiting team's pitching. There are nine or more innings in a regulation baseball game.
senses.example: It is a baseball tradition to sing "Take Me Out To the Ball Game" during the seventh inning stretch.

core.definition: One of the main divisions of a baseball game, in which each team gets a turn to bat and try to score runs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowel is short and quick, and the -ing ending is a light nasal sound, not a long 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a standard sports term, often used in casual conversation about games.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'inning' mainly for baseball, and fans often talk about 'the seventh inning stretch'. In cricket or other sports, the word has different meanings, so say 'baseball inning' if you want to be precise. In a bar or at a game, people say 'bottom of the ninth' or 'top of the third'.

distinctions.note: 'Period' is general and used for hockey or school; 'inning' is specific to baseball.
'Turn' is a general word for taking a chance, while 'inning' is the formal term for a unit of a baseball game.

collocations: the bottom of the ninth inning

examples.everyday: We left the stadium in the seventh inning because the traffic was terrible.
examples.professional: Our marketing campaign has entered its final inning, so we need to lock in the results this week.
examples.analytical: A baseball game is structured in innings, and each inning divides the contest into two halves, one for each team.

nuance.analogy: An inning is like a round in a boxing match, a fixed portion of the game that repeats until the end.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'innung', meaning a putting in, or a getting in, with reference to taking one's turn.
common_mistakes: Saying 'inning' for a single pitch or at-bat; an inning includes three outs for each team.
Confusing 'innings' (plural) with the singular form when speaking about a single turn.

inning.etymology: mistaken to be plural of the time period, not the entries of the batters/batsmen.

conversation.text: It's the bottom of the ninth inning, and the score is tied.
We got there in the third inning because of traffic.
They scored five runs in one inning.

senses.definition: Causing harm in a stealthy, often gradual, manner.
Intending to entrap; alluring but harmful.
senses.example: Hansel and Gretel were lured by the witch’s insidious gingerbread house.

core.definition: Harmful in a hidden or gradual way, so that the danger is hard to notice until serious damage has been done.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SID, the second syllable. The middle 'i' is a short 'ih' and the 'ee' sound is light, so the word has three syllables with the final 'us' reduced. Avoid stressing the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes a danger that is hidden, treacherous and hard to resist or detect.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'insidious' to describe slow, hidden threats such as disease, corruption, bias or addiction, especially in news, medicine and social commentary. It is a strong word, so it sounds dramatic in casual talk. Americans might say 'sneaky' or 'creeping' in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Sneaky is casual and often about small deceptions. Insidious describes serious, gradual harm that is hard to detect.
Subtle means delicate or hard to perceive, and can be neutral or positive. Insidious always implies harm.
Dangerous describes obvious risk. Insidious describes risk that hides behind an appearance of safety.

examples.everyday: My doctor warned me that high blood pressure is insidious because you often feel fine until something goes wrong.
examples.professional: Data drift is an insidious problem, since model accuracy can decline slowly without any obvious error.
examples.analytical: Bentham's panopticon exerts an insidious power, because the subject internalizes surveillance and disciplines himself.

nuance.analogy: An insidious problem is like a slow leak in a roof: nothing looks wrong until the ceiling collapses.
nuance.etymology: From Latin insidiosus, from insidiae, ambush, from insidere, to sit in or upon.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'invidious', which means unfairly causing resentment or unpleasant.
Stressing the final syllable, as in in-sid-ee-US.

insidious.etymology: From Middle French *insidieux*, from Latin *īnsidiōsus* (“cunning, artful, deceitful”), from *īnsidiae* (“a lying in wait, an ambush, artifice, stratagem”) + *-ōsus*, from *īnsideō* (“to sit in or on”), from *in* (“in, on”) + *sedeō* (“to sit”).

senses.definition: Capable of being understood; clear to the mind.
senses.example: Italian and Spanish are partially mutually intelligible languages.

core.definition: Clear enough to be understood; able to be grasped by the mind.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TEL. The middle syllables are reduced to schwa, and the ending is a syllabic 'bul,' so there is no separate 'ee' or 'ih' vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes whether something can be understood, without praising or criticizing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use intelligible in formal writing, academic work, and speech about clarity, such as 'an intelligible explanation.' In casual speech they would more often say 'understandable' or 'clear.' It is also used with a negative, as in 'barely intelligible,' to describe unclear speech.

distinctions.note: Understandable is everyday and common; intelligible is more formal and often describes speech or writing that can be decoded with effort.
Clear can describe anything easy to see or hear; intelligible focuses on whether meaning can be grasped.
Comprehensible is nearly the same but more formal and less common in American speech.

examples.everyday: The recording was so noisy that I could barely make out what he said, and it wasn't intelligible at all.
examples.professional: Please make the dashboard labels intelligible to non-technical managers, because they are the ones signing off on it.
examples.analytical: Wittgenstein suggests that a language is intelligible only when its rules can be shared within a community of speakers.

nuance.analogy: An intelligible message is like a clear window: you can see through it to the meaning behind the words.
nuance.etymology: From Latin intelligibilis, from intelligere, 'to understand,' from inter- and legere, 'to choose, read.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in 'in-tel-uh-JUH-bul.'
Confusing intelligible with 'intelligent,' which describes a mind rather than clarity of speech.
Using it as a noun; the noun form is intelligibility.

intelligible.etymology: From Middle French *intelligible*, from Old French, from Latin *intelligibilis*.

senses.definition: A small opening or space between objects, especially adjacent objects or objects set closely together, such as between cords in a rope, components of a multiconductor electrical cable or atoms in a crystal.
A fragment of space.
An interval of time required by the Roman Catholic Church between the attainment of different degrees of an order.
A small interval of time free to be spent on activities other than one's primary goal.

core.definition: A small opening or narrow space between closely set objects, such as the gaps between threads, cords, or atoms in a crystal.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the ending sounds like 'iss,' not 'ace.' The middle vowel is a short 'i,' so avoid saying 'in-ter-STEES.'

nuance.connotation: neutral. The word is descriptive and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'interstice' mainly in scientific, technical, or literary writing about small gaps. In everyday talk they say 'gap,' 'crack,' or 'space between.' Using it in casual conversation may sound overly bookish.

distinctions.note: 'Gap' is the everyday word for any opening or missing space; 'interstice' is more precise and specialized, usually for tiny spaces between closely packed parts.
A 'crevice' is a deep, usually rocky crack; an 'interstice' is a small space between adjacent things.

collocations: the interstices of a crystal lattice
through the interstices of the wall

examples.everyday: Sand had worked its way into every interstice between the deck boards.
examples.professional: The technician checked the interstices between the cable conductors for moisture before sealing the connector.
examples.analytical: Kant locates the interstices of human reason, the spaces where experience cannot fully determine knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Like the tiny spaces between bricks in a wall, where mortar goes.
nuance.etymology: From Latin interstitium, 'a space between,' from inter- 'between' and sistere 'to stand.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable (IN-ter-stice).
Using 'interstice' for a large gap or a break in time, where 'gap' or 'interval' is more natural.

interstice.etymology: From late Middle English *interstice*, from Old French *interstice* or directly from Latin *interstitium* (“a space between, gap, interval”), ultimately from *intersistō* (“to stand in between, to stop in the middle”), from *inter* + *sistō*.

senses.definition: In an intolerable manner; beyond endurance.

core.definition: In a way that is so extreme or unpleasant that it cannot be endured.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAH, as in intolerable. The middle syllables reduce to a quick 'luh-ruh', and the ending is 'blee', so avoid saying 'in-tol-ER-ab-ly'.

nuance.connotation: negative; it is an intensifier used to express strong frustration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use intolerably as an intensifier in complaints: 'intolerably hot,' 'intolerably slow.' It is more formal than 'really' but natural in casual speech about annoying situations. A natural reply is 'Tell me about it.'

distinctions.note: Nearly interchangeable; unbearably is slightly more common in casual speech.
Extremely is a neutral intensifier; intolerably signals the situation is actually impossible to endure.

examples.everyday: The traffic on the bridge was intolerably slow, so we took the back road.
examples.professional: The dashboard loads intolerably slowly on mobile, and customers have started to leave.
examples.analytical: Such a reading makes the text intolerably vague, reducing a precise command to a platitude.

nuance.analogy: Intolerably is like a sound so loud that you cannot stop hearing it.
nuance.etymology: Formed from intolerable (from Latin intolerabilis) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using intolerably as a verb or for a person; it modifies adjectives and verbs.
Stressing the wrong syllable; keep the main stress on TAH.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being intricate or entangled.
senses.example: the intricacy of a knot

senses.definition: Perplexity.
Something which is intricate or complex.
senses.example: There are many intricacies in the plot of this novel.

core.definition: The quality of having many small, interrelated parts or details that make something complex.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, IN. The middle vowels are reduced, and the final -cy is pronounced 'see'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can admire fine detail or complain about something overly complicated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use intricacy for designs, machines, systems, stories and arguments with many interlocking parts. It is common in both professional and general writing. In casual speech people often say the complexity or all the details. The word can be admiring, as in the intricacy of the carving, or critical, as in the intricacies of the tax code.

distinctions.note: Complexity is the general quality of having many parts; intricacy stresses fine, interlocking detail that requires care to understand.
Detail is a single small item; intricacy describes the whole pattern of many connected details.

examples.everyday: I love the intricacy of my grandmother's quilt, with hundreds of tiny stitches in every corner.
examples.professional: The intricacy of the billing rules makes the pipeline hard to maintain, so we should simplify it.
examples.analytical: The novel's power lies in the intricacy of its moral arguments, which resist any single reading.

nuance.analogy: Intricacy is like a watch movement: each small gear matters, and the beauty and difficulty come from how they all fit together.
nuance.etymology: From intricate, from Latin intricatus (entangled), from intricare (to entangle).
common_mistakes: Using intricacy as a countable noun without the plural intricacies when meaning several details.
Stressing the second syllable as in-TRIK-uh-see.
Confusing it with intricate, the adjective, in sentences that need a noun.

senses.definition: Lack of relationship with the topic at hand; lack of importance.

core.definition: The quality of not being connected to the topic at hand, or of not being important.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on REL, the first full syllable. The 'ir-' is 'ih-', and the unstressed middle vowels reduce to a quick schwa, so it sounds like 'ih-REL-uh-vuhns'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or dismissive. It suggests something does not matter to the discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use irrelevance in meetings, debates, and writing when they want to say a point does not apply. In everyday conversation people usually say 'That doesn't matter' or 'That's beside the point.' Saying a person is an irrelevance can sound harsh, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Triviality is about something small or unimportant in itself; irrelevance is about something not connected to the matter at hand.
Unimportance describes low significance; irrelevance describes lack of connection, even if the thing is important elsewhere.

examples.everyday: Let's stop talking about his old job, because that's total irrelevance to what we're deciding.
examples.professional: The committee rejected the proposal on grounds of irrelevance to our quarterly goals.
examples.analytical: Frege's argument turns on the irrelevance of psychological states to the logical truth of a proposition.

nuance.analogy: Like a key that is shaped for a different lock: it may be a fine key, but it does not open this door.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin irrelevans, from in- 'not' plus relevare 'to lift up, relieve, bear upon'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable; the stress is on REL.
Using relevance and irrelevance interchangeably when describing a point.

senses.definition: It irritates me, especially when repeated.

core.definition: Saying that something a person does or a noise irritates you, especially when it keeps happening.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NURVZ, and 'on' is reduced to 'ahn' or even 'un.' The words run together, so say it as one flowing phrase, and keep the r in 'nerves' American.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It expresses mild to strong annoyance, but it is casual and not usually cruel.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this expression in casual conversation about habits, noises or people's behavior. It is a soft criticism, so you can say it to a friend or roommate, but avoid using it with a boss or a stranger. A natural reply is 'Oh, sorry, I'll stop' or 'I didn't know, I'll try to be quieter.'

distinctions.note: Bug is even more casual and lighter; it is common among friends.
This is stronger and suggests the annoyance is almost unbearable.
Irritate is more formal and sounds clinical, so Americans rarely say it in casual talk.

collocations: that tapping gets on my nerves

examples.everyday: Your dog barking at the mailman every morning really gets on my nerves.
examples.professional: The constant pings from the chat tool get on my nerves, so I've muted it during focused work blocks.
examples.analytical: Dostoevsky's narrators often show how small irritations get on people's nerves until they turn into cruelty.

nuance.analogy: Like a sound that keeps tapping on a sensitive tooth, small and steady, until you can't ignore it.
common_mistakes: Saying 'gets to my nerves' or 'annoys on my nerves'; the natural phrase is 'gets on my nerves.'
Pronouncing 'on' as a full 'ON' in fast speech; it usually reduces to 'ahn' or 'un.'

conversation.text: He chews with his mouth open, and it gets on my nerves.
The dog is sweet, but when it barks all night, it gets on my nerves.
"Does the noise bother you?" "Yeah, it gets on my nerves after a while."

senses.definition: The hard white form of dentin which forms the tusks of elephants, walruses and other animals.
A creamy white color, the color of ivory.
senses.example: ivory:

senses.definition: Something made from or resembling ivory.
The teeth.
The keys of a piano; or, the white keys, as opposed to the black keys (ebonies).
senses.example: to tickle the ivories

senses.definition: A white person.
A die (object bearing numbers, thrown in games of chance).
Made of ivory.
Resembling or having the color of ivory.

core.definition: The hard, creamy-white material from the tusks of elephants, walruses and similar animals, used for carvings and piano keys.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EYE. The middle vowel is a reduced schwa that many speakers drop, so the word sounds like two syllables, and the final r is pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a material; positive when describing a color, where it suggests warm, soft elegance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ivory for the material and for the color, as in a cream-colored wedding dress. Because elephant ivory is restricted, the US has largely banned commercial ivory sales since 2016, so you may hear it discussed in news about wildlife conservation. Calling an antique piano key ivory is normal, but calling a modern one ivory may prompt a question about whether it is real or plastic.

distinctions.note: A tusk is the whole elongated tooth of the animal, while ivory is the dense material that the tusk is made of.
Off-white is a broad term for any slightly tinted white, while ivory names a specific warm, creamy shade.

examples.everyday: Her grandmother gave her a little ivory box that had been in the family for years.
examples.professional: Our design team chose an ivory background for the website because it looks softer than pure white.
examples.analytical: Ivory in the Hebrew Bible signals wealth and royal display, rather than the animal itself.

nuance.analogy: Ivory is like the warm, slightly yellowed white of an old piano, not the stark white of a new sheet of paper.
nuance.etymology: From Old French ivurie, from Latin ebur, ivory, related to the Egyptian word for elephant.
common_mistakes: Saying the first syllable as EYE-vor-ee with a strong second syllable instead of a quick, reduced middle.
Using ivory as a countable noun, as in an ivory for one tusk; the material is uncountable, so say a piece of ivory.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word is shen (שֵׁן), meaning tooth, used for ivory. Scripture mentions ivory as a costly luxury of royal and wealthy households. In 1 Kings 10:18 Solomon's great throne is made of ivory and overlaid with gold. In Psalm 45:8 the king's garments are described as coming from ivory palaces. In Amos 6:4 the wealthy of Samaria lie on beds of ivory, a sign of their indulgence that the prophet condemns.

ivory.etymology: From Middle English *yvory*, *ivorie*, from Anglo-Norman *ivurie*, from Latin *eboreus* (“in or of ivory”) adjective of *ebur* (“ivory”) (genitive *eboris*), from *yb* (“ivory, Elephantine”), from *ꜣbw* (“elephant, ivory, Elephantine”), from **leb-*.

senses.definition: Christ's voluntary abasement consisting of humanity and the simultaneous occultation of the Divinity.

core.definition: In Christian theology, the self-emptying of Christ in becoming human, taking the form of a servant and setting aside divine privileges.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'NOH', as in 'go'. The first vowel is a short 'ih', and the ending is 'sis' as in 'diagnosis'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and reverent in theology, suggesting humility and self-giving love. Some debates about its meaning are contested.
nuance.usage_note: This is a specialist term used in theology, seminary, and philosophy. Americans may use it more broadly for self-giving love. The related verb in Greek is 'ekenosen,' but English uses 'empty oneself.'

distinctions.note: Incarnation is God the Son becoming flesh, while kenosis describes the self-emptying or humility in that act.
Humility is a general virtue, while kenosis is the specific self-emptying of Christ.
In theology, condescension means God's gracious stooping down, without the negative modern sense of looking down on others.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study we talked about kenosis, how Jesus gave up status to serve others.
examples.professional: I'll teach a seminar on Philippians 2 that explores what kenosis means for Christology.
examples.analytical: Kenotic theologies debate whether Christ gave up divine attributes or simply refrained from using them, a tension shaping modern Christology.

nuance.analogy: Kenosis is like a king taking off his crown to wash the feet of his servants.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kenosis, 'emptying', from kenoo 'to empty', from the verb ekenosen in Philippians 2:7.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable ('KEN-uh-sis').
Thinking it means Christ ceased to be divine, which most traditions deny.
Confusing it with 'genesis' or 'necrosis' in sound.
nuance.biblical_note: Philippians 2:5-8 says Christ, though in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. The Greek verb is ekenosen, 'he emptied.' Other passages on the Son's humility include 2 Corinthians 8:9, where he became poor for our sake, and John 1:14, where the Word became flesh.

traditions.view: Kenosis is Christ's voluntary humility in the Incarnation, in which he remains fully God while taking human nature and suffering. Orthodox theologians reject any loss of divinity.

Kenosis is understood as Christ's humbling in assuming human nature and the form of a servant, without relinquishing divine nature, as taught by Chalcedon. The Church rejects views that Christ lost divine attributes.

Views differ. Some nineteenth-century Lutheran and Anglican kenoticists held that the Son gave up certain divine attributes, while Reformed and most evangelicals hold that he veiled or voluntarily limited their use without losing them.

kenosis.etymology: From Ancient Greek *κένωσις* (“emptying”) (see *keno-* and *κενό*), from *κενόειν* (“to empty”) (with reference to Philippians 2.vii, "But he emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, becoming as human beings are" – New Jerusalem Version).

senses.definition: To solve two problems with one single action.
senses.example: Biking to work kills two birds with one stone. It saves money traveling and will help to lose weight.

core.definition: To solve two problems or achieve two goals with a single action.

pronunciation.respelling: kil too burdz with wun STOHN
pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on STONE, the last word. 'With one' runs together as 'wi-thwun', and the z in 'birds' is voiced.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests efficiency and good planning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom about efficiency in meetings, errands and budgeting, for example 'If we merge these two meetings, we'll kill two birds with one stone.' A natural reply is 'Nice, that works.' Avoid it when discussing actual harm, because the image is violent.

distinctions.note: Multitask means handling several tasks at once; kill two birds with one stone means one action solves two problems.

collocations: kill two birds with one stone
a plan that kills two birds

examples.everyday: If you're going to the store anyway, grab my prescription too. Kill two birds with one stone.
examples.professional: Combining the sprint review with the stakeholder demo will kill two birds with one stone and save everyone an hour.
examples.analytical: Instrumental reasoning often promises to kill two birds with one stone, yet the trade-off between the two goals is rarely measured.

nuance.analogy: Like using one trip to the hardware store to buy both paint and brushes.
nuance.etymology: Recorded in English from the 1600s; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Omitting 'with', as in 'kill two birds one stone'.
Using 'a stone' instead of 'one stone'.

synonyms: feed two birds with one scone

conversation.text: I'll stop by the bank on my way to the gym and kill two birds with one stone.
Let's kill two birds with one stone and review both proposals in one meeting.
We visited my aunt during our Boston work trip, killing two birds with one stone.

senses.definition: A female relative.

core.definition: A female relative, especially one who belongs to the same extended family or clan.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KINZ, with a light secondary stress on 'woo'. The final syllable is a reduced 'mun', not 'man'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to formal. It sounds old-fashioned and appears mostly in biblical, literary or historical writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say kinswoman in everyday speech; they say 'cousin', 'aunt', 'relative' or 'family member'. You will see it in older translations and historical novels. In casual talk it may sound stiff, so use it only when you want a formal or literary tone.

distinctions.note: Relative is the everyday word for any family member, while kinswoman is formal or literary and specifically refers to a female relative.
Kinsman is the male counterpart, and kinswoman is specifically female.

examples.everyday: My aunt is my mother's kinswoman, but we just call her family.
examples.professional: The foundation's board included a kinswoman of the founder, so the committee disclosed the relationship.
examples.analytical: The Lukan narrative calls Elizabeth Mary's kinswoman, which places the two women within a shared family network.

nuance.analogy: A kinswoman is like a leaf on the same branch as you: different in shape, but growing from the same root.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cynn 'kin' and wif 'woman', meaning a female member of one's kin.
common_mistakes: Using kinswoman as a casual synonym for friend; it refers only to blood or marriage relations.
Stressing the second syllable (kinz-WOO-man); the main stress is on the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: In Luke 1:36 the angel tells Mary that her kinswoman Elizabeth has conceived in her old age, which connects the two women as relatives. The Greek word syngenis means a relative or kinswoman. The passage shows family ties shaping the story of John the Baptist's birth.

senses.definition: One of the Kohathites descended from the sons of Korah.

core.definition: The descendants of Korah, a Levitic family that served as temple gatekeepers and singers, and whose name appears in several Psalms.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ites sounds like 'ights'. Keep the r clear and the middle syllable reduced.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Korahites mostly in Bible study, worship music discussions and academic writing on the Psalms. It is a specialized term, and in conversation people usually mention the Psalms that bear the 'sons of Korah' heading instead.

distinctions.note: Kohathites were a separate Levitic clan that carried the holy objects, while Korahites were linked to temple gatekeeping and music.
Korah is the individual rebel leader, and Korahites are his descendants.

examples.everyday: At church, the reading mentioned the sons of Korah, and I wondered why so many psalms are attributed to them.
examples.professional: When I taught the Psalms, I pointed out that several psalms are credited to the Korahites, which tells us about their role in temple worship.
examples.analytical: The attribution of many psalms to the Korahites suggests a Levitic musical guild that preserved and transmitted sacred song within the temple.

nuance.analogy: Like a family of church musicians whose name appears on many hymnals, the Korahites are remembered through the songs that carry their name.
nuance.etymology: From Korah, with the Hebrew suffix for a descendant group.
common_mistakes: Using the singular 'Korahite' when the context needs the plural group.
Confusing the Korahites with the rebel Korah, who was their ancestor.
nuance.biblical_note: The Korahites (Hebrew bene Qorach, sons of Korah) were a Levitic family associated with temple service. 1 Chronicles 9:19 describes Korahite gatekeepers in the sanctuary, and 1 Chronicles 26:1 lists Korahites among the gatekeeping families. 2 Chronicles 20:19 mentions Korahites praising the Lord with loud voices. Several psalms, including Psalms 42, 44-49, 84, 85, 87 and 88, bear a superscription naming the sons of Korah.

senses.definition: Record a message for someone who doesn't answer the phone.

core.definition: To record a spoken or written message for someone who did not answer the phone or was not available.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on MES in message, and 'leave a' links smoothly into 'lee-vuh'. The middle vowel of message is nearly silent, so it sounds like 'MES-ij'.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a polite, routine phrase used in everyday phone calls.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Can I leave a message?' or 'Please leave a message after the beep' when calling someone who does not answer.
